utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, would the Registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor against Dusko Tadic case No. IT-94-1-AR72.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, this is an interlocutory appeal by the defence on the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. May I have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours I appear for the Prosecution together with Mr. Grant Niemann, Mr. Alan Tieger and Mr. William Fenrick. We are assisted at the bar table by Professor Theodor Meron and Mr. Payam Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My name is Orie, I am appearing for the Defence, Mr. President. I am assisted today by Ms. Cornee Royakkers who is assisting me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, before we start let me check whether the technical system works properly. Mr. Tadic, can you hear me properly in a language which is accessible to you. If you can hear me well could you please nod. Thank you. As we have started early this morning, we will recess at about eleven for about half an hour. Then I propose that we meet again here for the hearing at around eleven thirty until one o'clock, and then again after lunch break I propose that we meet again at two thirty until probably five or six but we will have a coffee break this afternoon as well. All right. Mr. Orie are you ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am. Mr. President, before starting my expos, I first would like to formally request you to introduce into the file the brief that has bee sent to the Tribunal by co- contributor, Mr. Vuyen. As I understand, a copy was received at the Tribunal so my request is whether it can be introduced formally into the file of this appeal proceeding.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Prosecutor. Have you any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will therefore put your document on record and it will be part of our record. This brief filed by Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, if I may proceed, I would like to give you a short outline of my expos of today. The first question I will deal with is the question to what extent the appeal is admissible. Is it admissible just on the truly jurisdictional matters as the trial chamber defined them or is it also admissible on the issues raised in connection to the establishment of the Tribunal itself. The second question I will deal with is the question whether the Tribunal is competent to review the resolution of the Security Council No. 827. The third question I will address is the question of whether there are any short-comings in the actual establishment of the Tribunal by the SC. I will do this briefly because it will perhaps be useless to repeat all the arguments that have been put forward before the Trial Chamber so I will make just short reference to that. Finally, I will address those issues of what are the determination of the Trial Chamber truly matters of jurisdiction and comment on the subject matter jurisdiction and relating matters. I finally will make a few remarks on evidence on this stage of the procedure. So let me come to the first question which is scope of the appeal. The question that needs to be answered is whether the appeal that has been filed by the defence also admissibly covers the issue of the legitimacy of the establishment of the Tribunal. In its response to the briefs supporting the appeal, in response of the Prosecutor to the appeal, the Prosecution submits that the first two points raised by the Defence do not relate to jurisdiction and that therefore rule 72b prohibits an interlocutory appeal in respect of these issues interpreted according to rule 73a 1. The trial chamber has made a distinction between matters properly described as jurisdictional, questions of time, of place and nature of the offence charged and matters that are not truly jurisdictional. I refer to the decision on page 4 para. 4 and page 19 para 45. The question of the lawfulness of the creation of this Tribunal has been characterised as not truly jurisdictional as a trial chamber. The term jurisdiction is not unequivocal and has several meanings. The transcript of the hearing of 25th July demonstrates already some confusion as to this term, page 19 - 20. The terminology is in need of clarification. Jurisdiction is not a single concept as Oppenheims International Law first Volume part 1, page 4,5,6 explains to us. It may take various forms. One of these forms is the power to regulate conduct by legislation. Fuller, in an article Jurisdiction over Offences with a Foreign Element in Assuninanda Treatise on International Criminal Law, volume 2, points out that jurisdiction may be understood in its limited procedural sense as in the expression jurisdiction of a court over offences with a foreign element, but also it could be understood in a more substantive sense of the legislative competence. Both meanings of this term are however, closely related since the jurisdiction of the court derives from the legislative competence of the state or in this case an international organisation. Stracht, which is a Dutch author on international law, gives six meanings apart from the one selected by the Trial Chamber for the term jurisdiction. Among this six the right of a state to issue abstract rules of a legal nature, notable enactment of legislation. The term "jurisdiction" as I am referring to now is usually referred to in French as "compétence compétence" and in German as "kompetence kompetence". It deals with the powers of the legislative organs. I may refer to the Lotus case, and it was clear in that case that the Turkish court exercised its jurisdiction and conformity with Turkish law, but the question was whether the Turkish legislative organs violated international law in creating these laws. That is regarded as a matter of the exercise by a state of its jurisdictional powers. The amicus curiae letter of the Juristes Sans Frontieres, unfortunately I have not received it yet in the English translation, but I am referring to the French text as we received it, this amicus curea brief supports this interpretation of Rule 73a1 page 6 of the amicus curiae brief even though this rule is not explicit in this respect. It is submitted, therefore, that the characterisation by the Defence of the issue of the lawfulness of the establishment of the Tribunal, the characterisation as jurisdictional is not erroneous. The terpretation of the term jurisdiction as given by the Defence stays within the scope of the wording and the meaning of Rules 72(B) and 73(A)(i). The appeal is hence submissible also in as far as it challenges the trial chamber decision concerning the lawfulness of the establishment of the Tribunal and the investment of it with jurisdiction, now, of course, I am using the word jurisdiction in the other sense, the jurisdiction of a primary nature. The next question I will address is the question on whether the Tribunal has competence to review Security Council resolution No. 827. The Trial Chamber has denied its competence to do so, to review Security Council resolution but at the same time deems it inappropriate to dismiss without comment the Defence contentions concerning the legitimacy of the establishment of the Tribunal by the SC. The approach adopted by the Trial Chamber is similar to the one adopted by the International Court of Justice in the Namibia advisory opinion. Nevertheless, the defence takes the decision that this way out of the problem is unacceptable in the present case. It is clear that the Tribunal is a unique organ and it has repeatedly been stressed that the entirely new situation in which it finds itself asks for new solutions. Since a tendency has been developed to find ways to judicially review the legality of the Security Council's resolution, the Tribunal has to fulfil its task in this respect. I may quote Mohammed Bedjaoui at a spot where he specifically mentions resolutions 808 and 827 before he concluded and I quote: "Indeed, whether one is in favour of it or not, the Council's freedom of appraisal finds clear textual warrant in the Charter. For that reason it could not as such very well be the object of legality control. On the other hand, as shown by the resolutions discussed above the same degree of immunity can surely not apply in the domain of the concrete activities that the Council is left to deploy as a result in particular, of its qualification of a given situation of Article 39 of the Charter. It is in this area of actions undertaken, or of the ways and means decided for having them carried out, that the need may arise and a proper place be found for testing the legality of the Security Council resolutions." I quoted om Bedjaoui and The New World Order and the Security Council, Testing the Legality of its Acts. The question of the competence to review the resolutions of the Security Council has been made subordinate in the approach taken by the Juristes Sans Frontieres in their amicus curiae brief. The first question is whether the Tribunal as an international judicial organ has the duty to investigate and decide upon its own its own jurisdiction. Where no clear decisions of the International Court of Justice can be invoked in which the legality of Security Council resolutions have been tested fundamentally, the test has until now always been provisional and in the sideline of the decision taken. The amicus riae brief points to many decisions in which international organs, the International Court of Justice included, have tested their jurisdiction over the case that was brought before them. Not testing the Security Council's resolutions, on the one hand, and a fundamental determination of its own jurisdiction, on the other, has never created, until now, a conflict. The legality and the binding effort of Security Council resolutions were in all known cases only relevant in order to define the obligations of the state parties in the conflict and to draw the legal consequences of these revelations of the states involved. In this case however, the issue of the legitimacy of resolution 827, is at a very legal basis of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The system of voluntary, or consequential jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice prevented that ever a conflict between the duty to freely determine its own jurisdiction over the case concerned and a reluctance to test the legality of the Security Council's resolutions ever arose. Since the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice cannot possibly derive from a resolution of the SC. This indicates that the Tribunal finds itself in a totally different position compared to that of the International Court of Justice. Having clarified this unique position, I will just shortly make reference to the substantive arguments that have been put already before the Trial Chamber to support the necessity of the review of the legitimacy of the establishment of the Tribunal. I would like to have them deemed, all these arguments to be repeated in full, but since your honours have access to the integral arguments to the transcripts of 25th and 26th July sessions of the Trial Chamber, for reasons of economy, procedural economy, I suggest that I just mention some of the main elements if I may. First, the basic right of individuals charged with criminal offences to be tried by a Tribunal established by law and not by an ad hoc Tribunal established by an executive, political organ. Second, the principle of legality as a primary requirement of every system of criminal law and procedure. Third, the inequality for suspected persons that results from the inconsistent and undemocratic decision-making process by the Security Council creating, or as a matter of fact mainly not creating, ad hoc Tribunals under the political control of the permanent members of the council. Fourth, the lack of power of the Security Council under the Charter of the UN to create judicial subsidiary organs and the imminent risk of the interference in the administration of justice by the Tribunal to be caused by new resolutions of the Security Council, being no consistency required and since no permanent judicial organisation independent from the existence of the actual conflict of Former Yugoslavia is in existence. Fifth, unjustified granting of primary jurisdiction to the Tribunal. Sixth, I would like to add, as I explained to you all the arguments put forward in the first instance, at least I hope that you will not force me to repeat them all because we will need all of Saturday and Sunday as well. But I add just a few remarks to that. I add to the summary that objections, emphasising the lack of power to establish the Tribunal were already raised in the International Law Commission in its 45th and 46th session by Prof. Gretna Arraign Ruin. Further, the lack of consistency violating the principle that equal situations have to be dealt with in an equal way, and the shortcomings of the statute in view of the observance of basic rights have been severely criticised by August Rainiest in an article in the Austrian Journal of Public and International Law in 1995. I will leave now the issue of the power to review the Security Council’s resolution and the substantive arguments why this resolution was not legally well founded and I come to perhaps the main issue, the subject matter jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: Mr. President? Mr. Orie, I have a question mark in mind. The argument that you have just been outlining is, of course, a very interesting [one], but I am just somewhat troubled by what would be the ultimate outcome if we follow you argument to its apparently logical end. We have this resolution of the Security Council establishing the Tribunal as it is today, which obviously is a political decision taken by the Security Council. You say that once this Tribunal has been created the Tribunal has the power, if not the duty, to review and test that decision of the Security Council, and ask those various questions that you have just enumerated. Assuming that we do that and that we would come to the conclusion that, say, under ground number three, you are right and, indeed we find that the Security Council has exceeded its powers under the Charter of the UN, what then would be the position? Would the answer have to be that this Tribunal finds that the resolution that created it was illegal, outside the powers of the Security Council and therefore the Tribunal would have to dissolve itself and say that it has been illegally created and therefore it cannot sit, cannot hear this prosecution, this particular indictment, nor any other indictment for that matter, and we all go back home saying we do not exist. Is that the logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That would be, perhaps, the final conclusion you would have to draw, but that is another problem I am not addressing at this moment but there is a problem of a vicious circle. Because if you are established, not lawfully, this would mean that even this decision could not be taken by an unlawful established Tribunal, therefore, whether you would just stop your activities, or whether you would give a decision saying that this Tribunal, at least these individuals sitting here, having been appointed by the UN to be members of a Tribunal cannot function because the legal basis of the Tribunal is legally defective. This is the true question that we are putting on the table, and the problem is that if we cannot put this problem on your table, on whose table could we ever put the problem? If there is no table at all then we have the situation where, even if you were convinced that the establishment is unlawful and if you would deny yourself the power, the competence to review the decision, that you would be in a very embarrassing situation. Of course, you would have to function in a Tribunal which is in your own view, perhaps, if you take no decision I will never know, but perhaps in your own view it is not a Tribunal established by law and not a Tribunal that could function under criminal law and proceed basic rights in criminal la and procedure properly to try individuals. That is my answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: Would not the General Assembly be the proper forum to raise that kind of an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: One of the problems of course is that the review of legality is, in my opinion, mainly a judicial task because the General Assembly is just as political as the Security Council is although of course, there are differences, no permanent members with defeat or power, we know that the General Assembly. . . I am not suggesting to you the solutions for the problem. Perhaps the General Assembly might be better, I am not saying good enough, but better than the Security Council. But it is not up to me to make suggestions as to how to make the legal basis of this Tribunal better, I just put the problem on the table that you will have to review the legitimacy of the establishment by the Security Council

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, in all constitutional systems of judicial review there are two ways of doing it. You either contest objectively, you ask for a general measure of review which means that if the court follows you it would decide that the contested act is illegal and hence does not exist or is not followed, or it could be simply in a more subjective way a demand for drawing the consequence of this illegality in a specific case. So the question here is, are you arguing in general about the constitutionality of the Tribunal or simply as an exception to jurisdiction. I know that the two are related but these are two different actions, in French you would say “deuce differences voices de reoccurs”. So I think you should enlighten us about your exact position in this respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think on the basis of the arguments put forward the consequence would be that our contesting the legitimacy of the Tribunal in this case would result, I am afraid that there is no other possibility, would result in the same decision in all other individual cases and that would in fact mean that generally the legitimacy of the Tribunal is discussed but of course I am acting in this case, I do not think that I have any standing generally to put on your table the problem whether the Security Council resolutions if not related to this case, would be illegal or not, but I think that we put forward in this case that as far as I can see now, I think it will have consequences for other cases as well, but it seems a bit difficult for me to say whether I am doing it in a general way or I am doing it in a more subjective way in this specific case. I am functioning in this case, but I am aware of the fact that this may have consequences for all other cases and so therefore in general the legitimacy of the Security Council's resolution is at stake as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, may I just ask you a question before you continue, before you carry on? Are you going to dwell on the six points you just mentioned one by one or will you move on to the next major section of your exposition, because I see from your nodding that you are not. You don’t intend to proceed to dwell on say on this principle of legality, the basic right to be tried by a Tribunal established by law and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is my intention in order to use our time in a economic way not to dwell on them and just refer to the transcript and the documents that have been used in the early instances, but if there be any questions about that, of course, I am quite willing to answer them because I am putting them on your table but not at this moment talking about them very well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in this case I would like to ask you a few questions about this very notion of right, basic right, of individuals to be tried by a court established by law. I think this is the gist or the lynch pin of your argument about the legality. I think the whole argument evolves around this basic right. You see the legality of the establishment of our tribunal from the viewpoint, not of the UN Charter, the UN Charter provisions, but rather from the viewpoint of the individual, of the defendant. Each, you say, you claim that each individual under the UN Covenant of Civil and Political Rights under the European Convention, the inter-American Convention has a basic right to be tried by a tribunal, established by law. All right, so my question is the following one. Of course you are aware of the case law of the various international bodies which are responsible for scrutinising the application of this three basic documents I have just mentioned and you know, of course, that when they have interpreted this expression, by law, they have always stated, most of the time actually, most cases they have stated that, that means by law means, by parliamentary act, by a piece of legislation, by a Statute by a piece of legislation adopted by parliament. So therefore my question is, ho can you in a way transpose from the national legal systems, where you do have separation of powers, you have a parliament, the executive and you have the judiciary, how do you transplant or transpose these notions from national law to international law, in other words, can you also argue in international law there exists a principle whereby everybody has a right to be tried by a tribunal established by law, because you can’t apply this notion of law in international law, you don’t have a parliament in international law and therefore you have a different system of legal sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now understand your question, Mr. President, of course this is one of the main problems, that is also the reason why in international situation a judicial organ should be established in such a way that it guarantees the same basic rights of the individual to be tried as good as possible. You will certainly know that quite a lot of authors deplored the establishment of the tribunal by a Security Council resolution, it wasn’t, they said it was an urgency situation quite a lot of people have expressed themselves that it would have been far better to establish the Tribunal by treaty, but there was no time, as a matter of fact there has been fifty years of time to establish a permanent tribunal, but nevertheless in this situation they said we have no time. And then we, I do agree with you that the constitutional elements of the United Nations are not the same as the division of constitution of powers in a national state, but this does not mean that the Security Council, which is an executive organ, can act both as a kind of legislator and both a transferring, not existing judicial powers to the Tribunal because the Security Council has now powers, so therefore again I do understand the problem and of course the problem has been solved in different ways, if you look at the International Court of Justice it was done by treaty, which is perhaps the best way of establishing whatever judicial organ. We also argued before the Trial Chamber that if the constitutional relations within the United Nations might not be fit to create a tribunal which could try individuals for criminal offences, that then perhaps the Charter of the United Nations should have been amended in such a way that there was an acceptable way in establishing the Tribunal. I think that I could put the question in a different way. If you say that the situation in the United Nations is not comparable to the national situations, then I could say that then the division of constitutional powers within the United Nations is not fit to establish a tribunal invested with jurisdiction over criminal offences. What we see, as a matter of fact is, that everyone wanted to have this Tribunal and that perhaps thetas at least then without perhaps division of defence, that there was no organ within the United Nations at that moment that could establish in an acceptable way, this means democratic etc. All the issues we dealt with before the Trial Chamber, then perhaps they should have come to the conclusion that it was not possible what actually happened is that the wish to have a tribunal had to find in one way or the other realisation and therefore I think the Security Council started interpreting their powers and perhaps unreviewable by any judicial organ in such a way that they were competent. I think this is putting things the other way around. I think you need to competence to establish a Tribunal and then you can do it. You cannot say that I need a Tribunal, I’ll just try to find in whatever corner, someone, of which I will say that he is competent to do it, and of course, I am aware that if you take this approach, and if you are desperately trying to find someone who can do the job that the Security Council would perhaps, because it can take minor decisions etc., and because its position within the constitutional framework of the UN made it not from a legal point of view, but from a point of view of realisation of the Tribunal, might have been the, I would not say the acceptable solution, but the best practical solution, its not acceptable in our view however.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, but still I have some doubts. You are aware of course, because there is a passage quoted in the decision handed down by the Trial Chamber, that when in 1949, in New York, Article 14(1) of the UN Covenant was being drafted - which lays down the principle whereby everybody has the right to be tried by a tribunal established by law - mention was made of the Nuremberg and Tokyo Tribunals which were ad hoc and yet which, it is generally agreed, gave the accused a fair trial in the procedural sense in most respects. So how would you comment on this passage, namely the authors of the UN Covenant considered that these two ad hoc tribunals were fully in keeping with the principle whereby everybody had the right to be tried by a tribunal established by law. So this is one point. The second point is, assuming there is, as you argue, a principle, this principle laid down in the three international treaties I mentioned before, the European Convention, the UN Covenant and the Inter- American Convention of Human Rights, Assuming that this is a general principle of law, would you classify this principle since we have to apply international law and we know that the sources of international law are listed in Article 30 of the, 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. How would you classify this principle, is it the principle, a general principle of law recognised by civilised nations or by the community of nations is a general principle of international law? In what, what is the legal standing of this principle? Therefore, at what extent is it binding on the Tribunal which is called upon to apply international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First I would like to respond to your question about the Nuremberg trial. I think that the situation of the IMT in Nuremberg has been very often misunderstood. It has been looked upon very often as an international Tribunal which, as a matter of fact, it was not in the true sense of this term. The four powers, the four allied powers, used their nationals jurisdiction and combined their existing national jurisdiction and combined their efforts and created a Tribunal. To some extent there was a situation where existing jurisdiction was reshaped in a different way. The main difference with the present situation is that there is no existing jurisdiction, there is no granting of powers to create courts, etc. Which there was in all of the four allied power countries. So I think that the comparison of this Tribunal with Nuremberg is very difficult one because the situation is totally different. The second question you raised as to the guarantees given by the European Convention of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Inter-American Covenant. I think that these are in these documents basic requirements, minimal requirements are adopted for the administration of criminal justice. I think they are not just conventional law any more. I think they finally got to the stage, because they are so basic, that if you violate these rights that you violate international law as well. I think they have got further reaching meaning by now. Apart from that I would like to draw your attention that it has been clearly the intention of the Security Council to apply these basic rights, on the other hand unfortunately the one key issue that was left that was the competence of the Security Council itself, was left out in the terminology, in the phrasing in the guaranteeing basic rights to the individual. So I would say that if these basic elements of fair criminal justice, which means not an ad hoc court, etc. Unless as you pointed out before the trial chamber, unless there is already a clearly accepted basis for making operative a special court in special circumstances. Then of course the parliamentary decision on whether these special courts can function at special times has been made far before the coming operative of these special courts. As I see it, they just left out one of the basic elements while they intended to apply all the basic human rights in the criminal law procedure

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you feel that in any case, even if the Tribunal has been set up by the Security Council which you call an executive body, or you say in your brief, an executive order, in any case the parliamentary body, namely the General Assembly, endorsed the setting up of this Tribunal by first of all electing the eleven judges sitting on the bench and subsequently by adopting the budget of this Tribunal. So in a way the Security Council decision was followed up by a stand taken by a sort of parliamentary body expressing the whole of the international community. And to this extent one could equate, mutatis mutandis, of course this process, this legislative process, to what happens within the national legal systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to draw your attention to the relation between the principal organs of the UN is not very clear as such. If we look, for example, at the decision in the Lockerbie case of the International Court of Justice, you see that there is a kind of rivalry between the International Court of Justice and the Security Council which is very difficult to handle. On the other hand, if you say that the General Assembly finally accepted the decision then, of course, the question arises whether the General Assembly can question the legitimacy of the Security Council. One of the problems is that whatever the General Assembly might have done, that we are dealing here not with states but with individuals. So therefore, there is no way the individual can, is not represented apart from by his state, but it is not like in a parliamentary system and I would very much like to see your reaction if in a national context a government would say, well, these courts are legitimate because I pay for it. There is no proper legislation, no proper decision making but from the mere fact that I am paying for it you may implicitly accept that it is OK as far as the government is concerned. I do understand that there are differences in the internal situation and the international situation, but I think that these basic decisions which have to be taken democratically, on whether this Tribunal can exist, can not be just made implicitly by either spending money on it or by electing judges. I mean it would, I think the relation between the Security Council and the General Assembly saying we are refusing to nominate judges because we do not like the position, I think that would be very difficult and therefore I think the whole question of the division and the relations of the constitutional powers in the UN could not be answered by me now, but the mere fact that there is an implicit acceptance of the existence of the Tribunal does not mean enough for me to say that I think it should be juridicial. Not a political test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, may I raise two questions? First, this Tribunal is established by resolution of the Security Council according to Chapter 7 of the Charter of the UN and other related articles. According to your view is it that the Charter of the UN is not law therefore it cannot be based upon to establish this Tribunal. This is my first question. And the second question is this, you seem to contend that this Tribunal has competence to review the legality of the Security Council resolution regarding the establishment of this Tribunal and the conferring to this Tribunal the primacy of this Tribunal over national courts. Now, could you cite any provision from the Charter of the UN or the Statute of this Tribunal which empowers this Tribunal to review the legality of the said resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first, if I may your honour reply to your first question. Whether Chapter 7 is law so that the Tribunal could be established by law under Chapter 7. If I would say it in a not very legal way I would say there was some law around, of course Chapter 7 gives power to the Security Council. It is also generally acknowledged that these are not unrestricted powers. What we think is that the Security Council could not use these powers in a way that has not really been thought of before and therefore if it would have been within the power of the Security Council to establish a court, invested with criminal jurisdiction, that this would have to be explicit because if you look at national systems then of course, there is some similarity between the Charter of the UN and national systems. I mean it is looked upon more or less as the constitutional law of the UN, I am aware of the differences but when we see that it would not be acceptable to create a criminal court without an explicit provision in law. And of course, Chapter 7 gives wide powers, it is not very specific in the way it granted powers to the Security Council. But I think that quite a lot of authors have asked themselves whether this was within the powers as they have to be understood as being given to the Security Council. I cited before, for example, Professor .., I forgot his name for the moment, but the remarks made by ... Just look it up, I think his name was Ruin. Well I did not find anywhere, nor in the legal literature, nor in any official comment the idea, apart from the first this time Yugoslavia problem, the idea that the Security Council could establish a judicial organ and for example how it required the Security Council to have judicial powers itself before it can transfer it to a subsidiary organ. So if you say is Chapter 7 law, I would say yes but, the question is whether these legal provisions are specific enough to justify this action by the Security Council. Let me then come to your second question. I have always problems in reading my own handwriting, you will understand. The second question was whether there was any power given in either the Statute or whatever other legal rule to review the decisions of the Security Council. As I pointed out before, there is of course, no such explicit legal provision giving you the power, so we are not relying on such a provision but the argument a contrario that if such a power has not been granted that it does not exist, seems not very convincing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I could ask, for example, how the Tribunal could create a criminalisation of perjury before this Tribunal. There is no power either in the Statute or in any other legal provision to do this. I think we are facing also the problem that where criminal laws and procedure in the national context are the result of a development of ages, and reviewed again and again by parliamentary organs, that, I would say, these Rules are established very quickly. I think, if I just look, the same is true perhaps for the rules of procedure in evidence. They have been amended already in one year, I think, two or three times -- the last amendment not even known to the Defence until recently. We are confronted with new Rules that were not already known to us. So I think that the a contrario argument is not valid because it seems not to be valid for the Tribunal itself. But, apart from that, it is a basic requirement because I pointed out to you the consequences of not reviewing; if you do not review, you would allow yourself to function in a Tribunal which you find yourself, perhaps -- as I said, I will never know -- unlegitimate. I think, apart from that it is necessary for the defendant, that it is necessary that political decisions are tested on the legal basis. I will point out later some comments to the quality, the legal quality, of decisions of the Security Council. I do not think that they are very much caring about legal subtleties. What they want is to create what they want to be there Therefore, I do not think that the absence of a specific provision giving you the competence to review the decision of Security Council is not a decisive argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: The action which was taken to create this Tribunal was under Chapter VII, proceedings, which you claim is political. By way of enforcement measure, the Security Council could also have passed a resolution that we take certain military measures and in that we direct that military Tribunals should be created to deal with persons who have committed serious offences against international humanitarian law. Would that not have been covered by this political decision? If so, then the question would be, what is meant by a judicial tribunal established by law? As I understand what this expression means, that a judicial tribunal can be created by a competent person or legal body of the state or organisation then in existence that can create a judicial body. Over many years the king would create judicial bodies in England and that was not any legal body. It is not necessary that a judicial body can only be created by a judicial body. What it implies is that it has to be created by a competent organ, body or a person then competent in law to create a judicial tribunal. The very fact that this Tribunal has been created ad hoc for a short period dealing with the particular territory and offences in that territory relating to violation of international humanitarian law is, perhaps, the very raison d'etre for that political decision. It was not that the United Nations was wanting t create a general court of international criminal justice for the people of the world, all nations with territorial jurisdiction expanding to almost all countries. That, perhaps, might be a case where safeguards like democratic processes and things like that might come in, or treaty matters. But since it was of a limited nature, for a limited purpose, for a limited time, to deal with that territory and people who had committed offences in that territory, that the very nature of this Tribunal to be ad hoc, to be temporary, so that it could be lifted no sooner peace came into operation, all this was a political process and a valid political process, because in a political process if the body which can create the judicial organ has the power, whether it be political, then it is correct. In so many eastern countries the legislators are totally disbanded and the President takes over all powers. From that point onwards all the decisions are just a single person's decision. You could treat half of them almost as political, but if he has the power he could create Tribunals. How do you react to this situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The main question is, what does it mean, "established by law"? If you refer to the past and say that kings established tribunals, courts, then I might say -- you are also referring to the Far East -- that might cast some doubts as to the democratic nature of both the decisions, the decisions given in the past by kings and, perhaps, the democratic values in some countries, whether it is absolute power in the hands of one person. If you ask me, if you say: "Well, it was not intended to create a permanent court for all countries", of course, I do agree with you, that is the discussion that went on for 50 years, and the United Nations finally did not succeed in establishing such a court. But that is, I think, exactly the problem, that it is a court, just a Tribunal, just for a limited period of time, limited offences, limited territory. That is especially the basic thought underlying the principle that Tribunals should have to be established by law; that it is not just a decision taken from one day to the other. "I do not think like that situation, so I create a court so that I can do something about it". That is exactly the kind of criticism that has been expressed against ad hoc tribunals. If, for example, in a country where the President has absolute power and when his whole family is in the banking business, he would say: "I will create criminal courts, not for the banking business, but for trade business and for whatever other kind", then exactly happens what should be prevented. What you need in order to administer criminal law properly is a continuing system which is not changed because, of course, there are always changes in the system, but you do not create it for specific events. We have pointed out before the Trial Chamber -- I could find it but it would take, perhaps, more than 10 minutes -- we have made reference to literature where they explain what the problems are with ad hoc courts. We explained, if we look to the past, that especially in the past in the law of extradition, this was not acceptable in the law of extradition because there was a fear that these kinds of ad hoc courts were influenced so much politically that they could not function properly and, therefore, that was not administration of fair justice. So if you say it was not mentioned to make a permanent criminal court, then my answer would be that that specifically is the problem for the Defence. We also pointed out there are hardly any decisions available in this respect. There is one decision by the European Court on Human Rights in Strasbourg dealing with a special court in Ireland. There at least they had a long-lasting basis to create these courts, although only under special circumstances these courts could become operative. What we contended is that at least prior to the existence of such a court it had been thought over, not in the specific threatening situation where there is a want for such a court, but there had been discussed in more abstract lines for on a more continuing basis by Parliament. If that answers your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you carry on, can I come back again to this so important notion of established by law, because I went through the legal literature and I came across the most authoritative work, it is called "Legislative Powers in the United Nations and Specialised Agencies" by Edward Yemin, 1969. There you find a broad definition of what is meant by legislative acts. Yemin says, and I quote: "Legislative acts have three essential characteristics: They are unilateral in form, they create or modify some element of a legal norm, and the legal nor in question is general in nature, that is, directed to indeterminate addressees and capable of repeated application in time". Then he goes on to show that actually the legislative process provided for in the UN Charter meets all these requirements. This is supported by a recent Article which you can find in the American Journal of International Law by Professor Kirgis, "The Security Council's First 50 Years". So, you see, I mean if you do not transpose mechanically the notion of law from the national legal systems or setting to international law, you have to broaden the notion of law of legislative process. I mean, I would accept, I wonder whether you would accept this definition of legislative acts as presenting these three features, because then on the basis of this definition Professor Kirgis concludes with regards to our Tribunal that, indeed, the establishment of our Tribunal does meet these three requirements because of this broader notion of law, because you do not have a parliament, of course, a proper parliament, in international law. The General Assembly is not a parliament. So I would like to have your comments on these definitions and then I promise that we will move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me, Mr. President, to ask you whether there would be an opportunity to have copies of these pages ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that I can comment on it later on because I find it a bit difficult to comment on literature which I have not read.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, may I raise another question? You contend that the Tribunal is by resolution? I think you contend this: If this Tribunal is established by a treaty, then it is established by law. This is your proposition. If this Tribunal is established by a treaty, it is established by law. As it is established by the resolution of the Security Council, you contend it is not established by law. Here the question is still, what is the definition of law? The definition of law, in the narrow sense, is that what is passed as legislative Act of the Parliament of a State. This is the narrow definition. In other words, sometimes the juries say: "Law is the command of the sovereign of a State". If you regard treaty as law, you use the word "law" in the broad sense and not in the narrow sense, because treaty is not command of the sovereign or the legislative Act of the Parliament. You use the word "law" here in the broad sense. If you can use the word "law" in the broad sense in the case of the establishment of this Tribunal by treaty, why can we not use the word "law" also in the broad sense, to regard the establishment of this Tribunal by the resolution of the Security Council also as law? You see, the resolution of the Security Council can also be considered as law in the broader sense, just as a treaty can be considered as law in the broader sense. How do you explain your contention that this Tribunal can only be established by a treaty? In that case, it can be regarded as established by law, but because it is established by a resolution of the Security Council, it cannot be considered as established by law. How do you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to answer your question, although it is on a very abstract level since I am a normal practitioner. I will try to do my utmost best. First of all, the example you gave, if you say: "Well, if the Tribunal would have been established by treaty, this would have been the broad sense of law". I think if you analyse the situation it might be composed of a mixed situation, because what you see is this entering into treaty relations is, on the one hand, command of the sovereign, at least a decision of the sovereign, whether he enters into treaty relations with other states or not is entirely within his sovereignty. So, to that extent, I do agree with you that this is law in the broad sense. On the other hand, we have to understand that law has even more meanings. For example, the law valid between the parties, the law of contract, for example. If we look at the law of treaties, there can be some comparison made to the law of contracts, and that is usually the rule, that is the way parties are using the law and then we are talking about, in national circumstances, law as provided by the state to its citizens. So, I think it is very difficult to say that in treaty relations this is the law in a broad sense. I think it has different elements. Apart from that, we are aware that as such the establishment of an international court should not be impossible. Therefore, we try to find out what would be the most acceptable way in doing it, if there is an acceptable way. Indeed, the example of the International Court of Justice shows that there is an acceptable way, but we have to understand that this Tribunal has entirely different powers from the International Court of Justice. There is a obligatory jurisdiction. My client cannot say: "I do not accept your jurisdiction" -- we are saying it a bit, as a matter of fact -- he cannot say: "I am not a party to your treaty so I am not subject to your jurisdiction". So, first of all, the situation is different, but what we intend to say is that in order to create a criminal jurisdiction, it is very important that all the requirements, all the basic requirements, of a fair administration of justice which are supposed to be guaranteed by the clause that it should be established by law are, if we compare the situation, not fulfilled in this situation. So I am not just pointing at law in its very narrow definition; I am pointing to the underlining basic thoughts under this notion of "established by law" which means you do not create Tribunals but not for banking division of your country. You do not create a Tribunal for specific offences in the specific area when you have political problems there. I mean, that is exactly all the drawbacks of the ad hoc courts as we have demonstrated or, at least, argued that these drawbacks do exist in the Trial Chamber were put forward in order to show that these basic requirements might be endangered by creating the Tribunal in a way that the Security Council did it, and that especially these dangers are countered by the requirement in the International Court of Civil and Political Rights, the European Convention, etc. by the requirement that it should be established by law. So, it is not an abstract argument, saying law must be in parliament, proposed by the government, voted by the parliamentarians. It is not that argument; it is to find a procedure to establish a Tribunal which is acceptable in the way that it complies with all the basic notions underlining the concept of "established by law". In my understanding, the powers of the Security Council, the very, very political decision-making in this organ and, of course, especially the veto powers of the permanent members, make clear that these requirements are not met. I am not choosing finally for the broad or the narrow sense. I am trying to find the underlining notions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Abi-Saab will ask you a question and after your answer we will break for a short recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, I think you answered my question by your last answer, but I will put it all the same because your answer has a mixture of three elements. You spoke of the treaty as a kind of a devolution of states of their own jurisdiction to an International Tribunal, so that makes it compatible with the rule as conceived from an internal law point of view, that the state which could have created the Tribunal would devolve that power b treaty to an international instance, so that is one. The second is, it is not simply established by a source, by a decision, which is obligatory. So you say it has to be more. As I understood what you said then, that "established by law" means -- we are here speaking, in fact, from the perspective of human rights “established according to the rule of law”, where guarantees are there, procedures are fair, etc. But if we go by that meaning (which I think is the more sensible meaning), then do not we have to examine each case on its own merits rather than just say that in this case we can imagine different legal system, different systems of division of powers within government etc., can produce Tribunals established according to the rule of law, although this procedure can be different from one case to another, if we use this sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I especially may answer the last part of -- I do not know what it was -- a question; I think it was a question. If you say well established by law would, in effect, mean established according to the rule of law, you gave a few examples, these examples were all within fair trial, etc. etc., that is not the basic element, although there are some elements in the Rules of procedure and evidence that might not meet that requirement. We pointed to some of them. I just pointed to an Article in the Austrian Journal of Public -- I will give you the sources later -- where there is some criticism as far as, for example, the right of appeal is concerned. But in this Tribunal there are several criticisms as to whether the Rules of procedure together with the Statute provide full guarantee of the basic human rights, but these examples were within the procedures that may follow before this Tribunal. When you say that the establishment according to the rule of law is, in fact, a requirement, then, of course, we would have to analyse exactly what are the basic elements necessary for creating jurisdiction. I just gave a few examples which are, of course, not decisive examples, but if you create criminal jurisdiction but not in the banking area where your family is very active and you are, on the other hand, creating criminal jurisdiction over the marketplaces in the town where the poor people are doing their trade, of course, that would not comply with fundamental elements, fundamental requirements, that have to be fulfilled in creating a criminal jurisdiction. For example, just to point out one of the problems in the Security Council is that, as you may know, it has been considered to create a criminal jurisdiction for crimes against war or crimes against humanity committed in the Gulf War. It has not been done. One of the basic requirements -- it is especially one of the things that is pointed out also in this Article in this Austrian journal -- is that the consistency -- it has been stressed again and again by the Prosecution -- that the Security Council does not have to be consistent. But, that is one of the problems, because if you say: "I do not have to be consistent in my actions. I am creating ad hoc tribunals wherever I need them, and when I do not need them or when there is a veto from one of the members, I do not create them", then, of course, one of the basic requirements, a I have just quoted this Article of August Rainiest, that equal situations have to be dealt with in an equal way also by the legislative organs might not be met by the Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I propose we stand in recess now until 11.30?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, I assume you now will take up the third point of your outline?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will now take up the subject matter of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then, if you do not mind, before you move on to this topic, may I ask you a question? Are you going to drop before the Appeals Chamber this issue of ius de non evocando, because I realise that you did not mention this particular item in the list of six items you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that we consider it to be a part of the basics underlying the principle that no-one can be tried by a Tribunal if it is not established by law. To that effect, it is the law who designates the competent judicial authority and to that effect it might be part of that. I will not address specifically on this point, but we are not dropping the issue, but we think it is contained in our position taken in the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, your Honours, I will come now to the grave breaches Article 2 of the Statute. The Tribunal has erroneously decide that, and I quote: "There is no ground for treating Article 2 as in effect importing into the Statute the whole of the terms of the Conventions, including the reference in common Article 2 of the Geneva Convention to international conflicts. As stated", I continue quoting, "Article 2 of the Statute is on its face, self-contained, save in relation to the definition of protected persons and things. It simply confers subject matter jurisdiction to prosecute what, if one were concerned with the Conventions, would indeed be grave breaches of those Conventions, but which are, in the present context, simple enactments of the Statute". I will quote a few lines further: "It follows that the element of internationality forms no jurisdictional criterion of the offences created by Article 2 of the Statute of the International Tribunal." I quoted pages 20 and 21 of the decision. No authority for this interpretation of Article 2 of the Statute was found by the Defence -- on the contrary. First of all, it should be noted that not even the Prosecution has taken the position that the internationality of the conflict is irrelevant for a jurisdiction of the Tribunal. I make reference to paragraph IIIA and especially pages 36 to 38 of the Prosecution's response to the Motion of the Defence on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. While discussing before the Trial Chamber the position of the government of the United States in the Amicus Curiae brief, the Prosecution qualified it as an interesting and novel approach to which it did not want to take a position. The transcript of 26th July, page 63 However, almost immediately afterwards -- I am referring to page 64 -- the Prosecution admits that it had some concerns about the argument that grave breaches could be committed in an internal armed conflict upon the basis of the argument put forth in the American brief. The Prosecution restricted itself in contending that the offences dealt with under Article 3, and not those under Article 2, of the Statute would fall within the scope of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal even if they were committed in an internal armed conflict. Secondly, one observes that the response of the Prosecutor to the brief to support a notice of interlocutory appeal very much concentrates on the issue of the internationality of the conflict, thus demonstrating the relevance of this issue. The history of the Statute also shows that the question of the internationality of the ongoing conflict in former Yugoslavia is relevant. The letter of 5th April 1993 from the permanent representative of the United States of America to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General contains a proposal under Article 10(a) to incorporate in the Statute a provision saying: "For this purpose, the conflict in former Yugoslavia on or after 25th June shall be deemed to be of an international character." Morris and Scharf who published a book called "An Insider's Guide to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia", page 58, described the fate of this proposal. They say: "Although this proposal might have greatly simplified matters, it did not find its way into the final Statute since this issue involved factual and legal questions that were considered to be more appropriate for determination by a judicial body. Thus the International Tribunal will have to determine the date on which a conflict became international", and I stress they say "a conflict", not "the conflict", "and, depending on whether the unlawful acts were committed prior to or during an international armed conflict, the crimes for which individuals may be held responsible". I am still quoting, "Deciding whether a particular conflict within Yugoslavia should be characterised as internal or international will not be a simple matter". I quote a few lines further: "Equally complicated is the characterisation of the hostilities between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs or between the Croatian government and the Serb minority in Croatia". The Secretary-General -- I am not quoting any more -- the Secretary-General of the United Nations qualified the Geneva conventions as the core of the customary law applicable in international armed conflict, and points out that serious violations that qualify as grave breaches involve criminal liability. No reference whatsoever is made as to the applicability, in view of Article 2 of the proposed Statute, of the grave breaches provisions in an internal conflict. Other learned writers take a similar position. I may refer to an Article of Carsten Holweg called Kriegsverbrechen in Ex Jugoslawien vor dem neuen UN-Tribunal, Schriftenreihe der Deutschen Gruppe der AAA -- I have an abbreviation but I do not know what i stands for any more, but I will give you the source to you later. Carsten Holweg indicates that 1st January 1991 was chosen as the safe commencing date of jurisdiction of the Tribunal because one had difficulties in finding a decisive date on which the conflict became of an international character. He denies criminal responsibility under Article 2 of the Statute unless the offences have been committed in an international armed conflict. I would also like to quote Professor Meron -- he will be aware of what he has written before -- after he quoted the Secretary-General of the United Nations where the Secretary-General says: "The international tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law". Professor Meron states: "Whether the conflicts", and he is using the plural, "in Yugoslavia are characterised as internal or as international is critically important". He also explains why. He says, and I quote again: "Violations of common Article 3 do not constitute grave breaches giving rise to universal criminal jurisdiction." A similar position has been taken by Professor Kalshoven. Unfortunately, his contribution to a conference has not been published but we provided already copies and we will provide copies. He says: "The conclusion seems inescapable that by employing the identical terms as are found in the 1949 Conventions, Article 2 of the Statute confines the competence of the Tribunal to the situations where the grave breaches provisions of the conventions are applicable, i.e. i situations of international armed conflict. Article 2 does not therefore", and I am still quoting, "give the Tribunal competence to deal with violations of the basic norms of International Humanitarian Law set forth in Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions which alone are applicable in internal armed conflict". Professor Schutte -- he is also Dutch -- also expressed himself on the issue during the same conference and he says: "From that perspective it to be noted that Article 2 of the Statute appears to be relevant only where it has been established that the armed conflict in connection with which the alleged offences have been committed has the status of an international armed conflict, within the meaning of Article 2 common to the 1949 Geneva Conventions, this is an armed conflict between two or more High Contracting Parties to the Conventions". The Commission of Experts expressed in their final report also the relevance of the internal, or the international character of the conflict. By the way, the report also expresses that more conflicts were going on in the former Yugoslavia. As to the grave breaches the report reads: "The grave breaches provisions in the Geneva Conventions and Protocol I are only relevant during an international armed conflict". One might argue that the Commission dealt with Treaty Provisions while the Trial Chamber decided that it applied customary international law. This is, however, incorrect, since it becomes obvious that the Commission of Experts takes the same position, requiring an international armed conflict, if the Commission deals with customary law under Article 3 of the Statute. I will come to that later. Further, I would like to emphasise that at the time of the delivery of the final report, the Commission of Experts was fully aware of the content of the Statute of the Tribunal. The final report was in 1994 while the Statute was known already for quite some time. One could wonder while the Trial Chamber has adopted a view so different from the interpretations formulated by the doctrine and by the Commission of Experts. We, therefore, have to analyse the exact reasons why the Trial Chamber held that Article 1 of the Statute empowers the Tribunal to interpret Article 2 as self-containing, rather than as referential to the Geneva Conventions. I quote from the decision, paragraph 51: "The Report of the Secretary-General makes it clear in paragraph 34 that it was intended that the rules of international law that were to be applied should be 'beyond any doubt part of customary law', so that problems of non-adherence of particular States to any International Convention should not arise. Hence, no doubt, the specific references to the law of the Geneva Conventions in Article 2 since, as the Report states in paragraph 35, that law applicable in armed conflict has beyond doubt become part of customary law". Our comment: First of all, it needs attention that paragraph 35 of the report of the Secretary-General, to which reference is made by the Trial Chamber, relates to the Articles 2 to 5 as a whole. Therefore, it uses wordings that are valid for all these articles. Since, for example, Article 5 of the Statute covers crime against humanity committed either in an internal or in an international conflict, the Secretary-General could not have used the term "International armed conflict" in paragraph 35 since it would not cover the whole of Articles 2 to 5. In paragraph 37, however, where the Secretary-General exclusively deals with the grave breaches provisions as enumerated in Article 2 of the Statute, he specifies what is valid in that respect. They provide the core of the customary law applicable in international armed conflicts. Zacklin, who may be considered to know something about the history of the Security Council resolution, justly interprets the function of Article 2 of the Statute as follows, and I quote: "The list of international humanitarian law violations that are of undoubtedly customary international law nature was further limited to those which have customarily entailed the criminal liability of the individual, and includes, according to Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations of the laws of customs of war, the crime of genocide and crimes against humanity." The Defence, therefore, submitted that the scope of Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute is not widened by Article 1 but, on the contrary, that the scope of Article 1, using rather general terms, is further limited by the Articles 2 to 5. This also explains the implicit acceptance of all authors cited that the reference to the grave breaches provisions includes the requirement that they are committed in an international arm conflict. Under customary law, these grave breaches exclusively entail criminal liability for the individual if committed in an international arm conflict. It seems to me that the Prosecution has interpreted Article 2 accordingly in the proceedings before the Trial Chamber. In its comment to resolution 808 the International Committee of the Red Cross already expressed its view on the limitations of the criminal liability for violations of international humanitarian law. I quote again: "It is not up to the ICRC to decide, on behalf of the international community, which part of the past and the present armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia are not covered by the law of international armed conflicts. However, with regard to such qualifications, the ICRC wishes to underline the fact that, according to international humanitarian law as it stands today, the notion of war crimes is limited to situations of international armed conflict." The Defence is of the opinion that the matter has been defined wrongly by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 52 of the decision, where the Trial Chamber emphasises that it is truly a matter of the attribution of jurisdiction to States not involved in the conflict, and on a different basis here to the Tribunal. The requirement of the existence of an international armed conflict is essential for the individual criminal liability under international law (whether it is treaty or customary law) and, therefore, it is essential for the principal nullum crimen sine lege as well In view of the sincere wish of the Secretary-General to limit the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to violations of International Law that are beyond any doubt part of customary law, it is submitted by the Defence that Article 2 of the Statute should be interpreted as limiting the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to grave breaches committed in an international armed conflict. One of the consequences of this position taken by the Defence is that the Defence holds that the Trial Chamber erroneously failed to establish whether the conflict at the relevant time and place was of an international character. The Trial Chamber has further deemed it unnecessary to decide whether the grave breaches provisions were operative, due to special agreements between the parties. This question, however, becomes relevant again if the Appeals Chamber would decide that Article 2 of the Statute requires the fulfillment of all conditions under the Geneva Conventions to make the grave breaches provisions operative. The Prosecution has argued before the Trial Chamber that the parties to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina have agreed to apply the grave breaches provisions by means of special agreements pursuant to common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. Reference in that respect is made by the Prosecution to the agreement of May 22nd 1992 between the representatives of Mr. Izetbegovic, both in his capacity as President of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and President of the Party of Democratic action, b Mr. Karadzic as President of the Serbian Democratic Party and by Mr. Brkic as President of the Croatian Democratic Community. The Defence contended before the Trial Chamber (and still does before your Chamber as well) that the agreement of 22nd May 1992 under common Article 3 does not refer to Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV, so that this agreement only provides for a limited protection of civilians in the context of common Article 3. Article 3 of the Agreement on the release and transfer of prisoners of October 1st 1992 is not to be understood, as the Prosecution has argued, as a confirmation of the implicit consensus by the parties to the agreement of May 22nd 1992. It is obvious that the parties might have developed different views as to the character of the conflict. One of the parties might have considered it to be of an international character and, therefore, might have intended to initiate investigations on or prosecutions for violations of the grave breaches provisions. This does not necessarily mean, however, that the other party, or parties, agreed to this characterisation of the conflict, and on the applicability of the grave breaches provisions. The party, engaged in such prosecutions, reserved the right under the October 1st agreement not to release the prisoners that were accused of or sentenced for grave breaches. It cannot be interpreted as a confirmation of an implicit consensus against the precise wordings of the May 22nd agreement, but the agreement just limits the obligations of the parties in view of a potential de facto situation where, in fact, prosecutions had been initiate against individuals charged with grave breaches. As far as the unilateral declarations of 27th August 1992 are concerned, they did not constitute an agreement under common Article 3, they not being a declaration of an international legal nature. The documents were signed by two parties without any reference as to the capacity of the person signing the document. Furthermore, the wording of the unilateral declaration leaves no doubt as to the intention to engage in an undertaking for the future. As you will know, there are no charges brought against Mr. Tadic after 27th August. No retroactive effect can derive from its wordings. I will now leave the grave breaches and come to the war crimes. There is a striking similarity in the way the Trial Chamber dealt with the jurisdiction under Article 3 of the Statute and the way it dealt with the charges brought under Article 2 of the Statute. It is clear that the enumeration of acts in Article 3 of the Statute is not exhaustive. Since it was the intention to cover all war crimes under customary international law by Article 3, it was not possible to list them all without the risk of forgetting a few. To that extent, international customary law plays an important role while interpreting Article 3 of the Statute. But here again the Trial Chamber has limited itself to the substantive norms and neglects sources of international law (and since the Trial Chamber stresses again and again that it applies customary law instead o conventional international law, this would have to be international customary law) characterising the violations of the laws and customs of war as crimes in the sense that these violations entail an individual criminal liability under customary international law. Even if it is true that in the Nicaragua case the International Court of Justice recognised the applicability of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions (it seems that by mistake the decision reads in paragraph 71, Article 1, I think, referred to, it is meant to refer to Article 3) to non-international armed conflicts, this only pertains to the obligations thereof and not to the individual criminal liability for violations of common Article 3. The Secretary-General referred rightly to the prohibitions contained in common Article 3 when drawing the attention to the decision of the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, not to the characterisation of violations as crimes under international customary law. No opinion juris sive necessitatis to that extent has been established by the International Court of Justice. I again on this issue have to quote some eminent authors on the subject matter, mainly the same as I quoted before but they dealt with the whole matter. First, Shraga and Zacklin, I quote: "In its interpretive statement upon the adoption of Security Council resolution 827 (1993), the US delegate declared that the 'laws and customs of war' in Article 3 of the Statute refer to 'all obligations under humanitarian law agreements in force i the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time the acts were committed, including Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and the 1977 Additional Protocols to these Conventions'. Article 3", says Zacklin, "of the Statute contains, however, provisions which meet the cumulative criteria of undisputed customary international law nature, and of individual criminal liability, and although common Article 3 of the four Geneva Conventions represents a customary international law standard of minimum human conduct applicable in internal armed conflict, it does not entail, under the Geneva Conventions, the individual criminal liability of the perpetrator of this crime. The Article prohibits violence to life and person, in particular, murder of all kinds, cruel treatment and torture, taking of hostages, outrages upon personal dignity, humiliating and degrading treatment, and the passing of sentences and the carrying out of execution without previous judgement pronounced by a regularly constituted court affording all the judicial guarantees. Note however", says Zacklin, "that the crimes of murder, torture and the taking of hostages are also crimes against humanity which under Article 5 of the Statute may be committed in under armed conflict whether international or internal in character." James O'Brien (although he thinks that the conflict was of an international character and that, therefore, common Article 3 is applicable) stays apart from the question. I quote: "Whether or not it is well established international law that common Article 3 give rise to individual criminal responsibility ...", and then he continues but it is at least a question for him. I quote Kalshoven: "Here again, therefore, the competence of the Tribunal appears to go no further than to deal with the violations of the laws and customs of war committed in situations of international armed conflict." I quote Schutte again: "As far as Article 3 is concerned, Professor Kalshoven has shown that its provisions are taken from the laws and customs of war applicable in situations of international armed conflicts only. Even if one would construe the Article as not only based on the 1907 Hague Regulations on land warfare -- as he does -- but also on some of the provisions of the 1977 Protocol I, its application would remain limited to situations of international armed conflicts. I quote again Theodor Meron: "Violations of common Article 3 do not constitute grave breaches giving rise to universal criminal jurisdiction. Where any part of the conflict deemed internal rather than international, the perpetrators of even the worst atrocities might try to challenge prosecutions for war crimes or grave breaches, but not for genocide and crimes against humanity". I must add one thing to this quotation. I do understand the word "perpetrators" as used by Professor Meron as meant to refer to "those accused of having perpetrated", since he is referring to a stage of the trial where it has not yet established whether the defendants are guilty and, therefore, are perpetrators. Morris and Scharf are also very clear on this point. They say: "The concept of individual criminal responsibility for grave breaches humanitarian law or war crimes does not extend to internal armed conflicts". The position that has been taken by the ICRC, as I quoted before, is both valid for grave breaches and violations of the laws and customs of war. I now come back to the final report of the Commission of Experts in paragraph 54. I read the whole very short paragraph.
