The report says: "It must be observed that the violations of the laws and customs of war referred to in Article 3 of the Statute of the International Tribunal are offences when committed in international but not in internal armed conflict." The Trial Chamber has evoked both Green and Bassiouni support its decision by quoting their definitions of war crimes in which no requirement of an international conflict is contained. I would like to quote the same authors at those places where they clarify their position when they explicitly deal with the issue at stake. The first quote, Bassiouni: "The essential difference between acts deemed war crimes and those deemed 'crimes against humanity' is that the former acts are committed in time of war against nationals of another state, while the latter are acts committed against nationals of the same state as that of the perpetrators." I quote Green as to the criminal liability under common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions: He says: "Article 3 also provides that the ICRC or some other impartial humanitarian organisation may offer its services to the parties in a non-international conflict and to emphasise the humanitarian intents of the Article it calls on the parties to 'endeavour' to reach agreement among themselves to bring other articles of the Convention into operation. This may result in introducing grave breaches clauses and thus authorise trials for war crimes". It is clear that Green does not envisage such trials for war crimes if no such agreements are concluded between the parties. This illustrates that the violations of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions as such do not entail individual criminal liability. Green, therefore, shows to be surprised by the appointment of the Committee of Experts by the Secretary- General. I quote again: "Then, in October it reaffirmed the earlier resolutions, expressed increased concern at the continuing reports of widespread violations of international law, including practice of 'ethnic cleansing' and instructed the Secretary-General to appoint a Commission of Experts to investigate and collect information concerning alleged crimes in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and to make recommendations as to further actions to be taken to deal with these alleged crimes. This was", I am still quoting Green, "an interesting development in view of the fact that, for the main part, most of the allegations arose from activities by one group of Bosnians against another so that there was no international armed conflict in progress, and Protocol II concerning the law in non-international armed conflicts makes no reference to the Conventions, breaches of the Protocol or to the law of war, and makes no provisions for punishment. To the extent that any such atrocities were committed by, for example, Serbian Serbs, especially if this was due to negligence in failing to prevent or complicity by the Serb government, then it might be possible to argue that the laws of international armed conflict would apply to them". That is the end of the quotation of Green. The Trial Chamber is, nevertheless, paying a lot of attention to the criminal character of the violations of the laws and customs of war. It does, however, not establish beyond doubt that the individual criminal liability exists under international customary law. The example of the International Military Tribunal of Nuremberg is in no way conclusive, since it only dealt with war crimes that were, for historical reasons, embedded in a clear situation of an international armed conflict. Furthermore, the IMT was exercising combined jurisdiction on behalf of the Allied Powers, not international jurisdiction in the true sense of this term. The Lieber Code, to which reference is made by the Trial Chamber, was intended to serve national purposes. It was promulgated by President Lincoln in 1863 as law, but only binding upon United States forces. If a criminal liable was contained therein, it was the sovereign expression of a government that it wanted to apply this domestic legislation under the circumstances of the American Civil War. When the Trial Chamber invokes the German Military Manual to support its decision, it refers to Theodor Meron. It caused me -- it always causes me to verify the sources when Professor Meron is involved -- to verify this source. I would like to quote the following lines of Meron's article as well, and not just the ones referred to by the Trial Chamber. He writes: "The draft Canadian Forces manual takes a different approach but agrees that violations of common Article 3 and Protocol II should be prosecuted, 'While non-application (of common Article 3) would appear to render those responsible to trial for war crimes, trials would be held under national criminal law, since no "war" would be in existence'." So, domestic legislation criminalising violations of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions committed in an internal conflict, and certainly not when state practice shows quite different legal opinions underlining it, does not result in an individual criminal responsibility or liability under customary international law. The Prosecution agrees with the Trial Chamber that it is not necessary to undertake to classify the conflict as international or internal, but they do it on different grounds. Where the Trial Chamber found it unnecessary because of the effect of customary international law, the Prosecution holds that it is unnecessary because the Security Council itself has already classified the conflict as international. It is surprising that the Prosecution is of the opinion that it just can refer to the classification of the conflict by the Security Council and thus is release from its obligation to prove the existence of a situation which would require a mixed valuation of law and facts essential to the question of whether or not the Tribunal has jurisdiction over the alleged acts. This position violates the independence of the Tribunal. It would subordinate the Tribunal to the Security Council, a political organ, also where the establishment of relevant facts and their legal appraisal is concerned. The jurisdictional questions have to be tested independently by the Tribunal, applying criteria that belong to well established international law, and after having established the relevant facts. The political character of the Security Council's attitudes towards the conflict in the former Yugoslavia has been noticed by Green where he writes, I quote: "During 1991, 1992 and 1993 both the European Community and the Security Council have tended to regard some civil conflicts arising from the efforts of part of a federation to break away from the established state as if they were international conflicts, as has been the case in Yugoslavia." The question whether the conflict can be classified in its entirety is disputed. To draw the conclusion that, because of its reference to the grave breaches provisions, the Security Council's resolutions have to be interpreted as an expression of its position that the conflict must be viewed in its entirety, is not justified, and that is exactly what the Prosecution does. It may be that the Security Council, perhaps for goo reasons, intended to classify parts of the complicated conflictual situation as resulting in an international armed conflict, and that, therefore, acts committed in the context of these parts of the conflict have been regarded as having been committed in such an international armed conflict. This does not mean, however, that the global approach of the Security Council is decisive for the valuation of specific acts that might not show whatever nexus with this ongoing international conflict. Again many authors have expressed their view that the Yugoslavian conflict developed in different areas and in different times as separate conflicts. I quote again Morris and Scharf: "The Secretary-General's report does not take a position as to whether the various conflicts" -- he is also using the plural -- "within the former Yugoslavia could qualify as international in character for purposes of the applicable law as of a particular date". A few lines further: "The conflict in the former Yugoslavia has internal and international elements. There was only one country until Slovenia declared independence on June 25th 1991. Thereafter, some fighting involved intranational conflict, particularly Bosnian against Bosnian, and some international elements, such as the Yugoslav National Army (the JNA). The JNA was officially withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the spring of 1992, ostensibly leaving only internal combatants there. It is possible (but not correct)" -- I have to clarify myself, when I just said that I was quoting again Morris and Scharf, a few lines further, I started quoting O'Brien He says: "It is possible (but not correct, as I note below)" -- this is also a quotation of O'Brien -- "that the Tribunal might determine the conflict to be internal; noting that it was not to make new law, it could refuse to apply the law of international armed conflict to some or all of the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the spring of 1992 when some of the worst war crimes appear to have taken place." I clarify myself. I am quoting O'Brien. I am aware of the fact that he finally comes to the conclusion that it was an international armed conflict, but I am quoting him mainly because his Article shows the relevance of the question. So, although O'Brien takes the position that the conflict should be regarded in its entirety, he provides us with information that allows to draw an opposite conclusion as to the different conflicts ongoing on the territory of Yugoslavia. Since it might be a bit embarrassing for Mr. Fenrick, I will not quote him again, but instead I will quote Mr. Green. Mr. Green writes: "In fact, in the recommendations put forward by Commander Fenrick, a member of the Commission, on the Legal and Policy Issues related to Commission of Experts, it was recommended that activities occurring in Bosnia-Herzegovina during an armed conflict prior to 6th April 1992", when Bosnia-Herzegovina was deemed to have become an independent state, "should be considered as occurring in an internal conflict, while activities occurring between 6th April 1992 and May 1992 should be considered as occurring in an international armed conflict, and those occurring after 19th May 1992 should be considered as occurring during an internal armed conflict." It is submitted by the Defence that several conflicts existed in the territory of former Yugoslavia, and that they have to be taken separately into consideration by the Tribunal while deciding on the subject matter jurisdiction over the charges brought against this defendant. It has been the intention of the Security Council that the Tribunal should decide by its own when the conflict in Yugoslavia became international. If we look at the possible dates that have apparently been considered as a starting point for the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, I would like to quote again the article of Shraga and Zacklin. They write: "In the search for a specific date within the general reference to 1991, three dates were considered, each referring to a specific event to which the beginning of the dissolution process of the former Yugoslavia could have been attributed: 25th June 1991, the proclamation of independence by Croatia and Slavonia; 27th June 1991, the intervention of the Federal Army in Slovenia and 3rd July 1991, the outbreak of clashes between Serbian and Croatian militia. The Secretary- General opted, however", I am still quoting Shraga and Zacklin, "for a neutral date which would not carry with it any political connotation as to the international or the internal character of the conflict, with the legal implications that such a determination would have entailed for the choice of the applicable law In addition, information made available to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 1 of the Security Council resolution 780 (1992) suggested that crimes falling with the jurisdiction of the Tribunal might have been committed against Serbian population before June 1991. The choice of 1st January 1991 was, therefore, intended to embrace all crimes by whomsoever committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1991, and to convey an image of complete neutrality and impartiality in the Yugoslav conflict." It becomes clear from this that the armed conflicts that arose after the proclamation of the new states were of major importance for considering the conflict to have become international. No mention whatsoever is made about the development of internal conflicts between the different ethnic groups (Muslims, Croats, Serbs) within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It might not have been of major importance to the Security Council when exactly the conflicts became of an international character. Jurisdiction was granted as well for crimes that could have committed in internal armed conflict, or even without an armed conflict at all in Article 4 of the Statute, but genocide is not relevant in this case. Under these complex circumstances, the Tribunal has the duty not only to decide when the conflict became international, but also whether the different parts of conflict, and I would rather say the different conflicts, became international at all at relevant places Where it has been argued by the Prosecution that the Security Council is not bound to exercise its powers in a consistent way, quite of a sudden the consistency of the decisions of this organ is invoked when it comes to the references to the applicable law as an indication whether an internal or an international armed conflict exists. I may refer to the observations of Green, demonstrating that exactly here the Security Council was not acting consistently in his opinion by defining the internal conflicts as international conflicts as well. As to the facts known at that time to the Security Council, the Defence, first of all, observes that these were the very facts that were available as well to Commander Fenrick when he classified the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina as he did in 1992. Moreover, Commander Fenrick (and the other learned writers I quoted as well) had not only these facts at their disposal, but also the resolutions of the Security Council that have been invoked by the Prosecution. Nevertheless, they did not interpret at that time these resolutions as demonstrating that the Security Council viewed the conflict within Bosnia-Herzegovina as an international one. Apart from the fact that the Defence is of the opinion that the resolutions cannot be admitted as evidence since they lack the precision necessary to decide upon the jurisdiction in this particular case, they are also the results of a political decision-making process, and they are not convincing either. Resolution 713, dated 25th September 1991, at that date, according to the Badinter Commission, none of the states stemming from the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, especially not Croatia and Slovenia, succeeded the SFRY. Therefore, the Security Council could not but refer to Yugoslavia because there was nothing else at that point. Resolution 757 consistently makes a distinction between the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in other parts (or republics) of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The mere fact that the different conflicts, all of them consequences of the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, are dealt with in one resolution is not a convincing argument. First of all, it would have been silly and impractical to adopt a separate resolution for all of the ongoing conflicts. Does the fact that, just for example, resolution 752 exclusively deals with the problem within Bosnia-Herzegovina mean that the Security Council expresses as its view that it is not any more one of the conflicts stemming from the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Of course it does not, although it gives some indication as to the individuality of the Bosnian conflict. The call for the collation of substantial information relating to violations of humanitarian law, including grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions being committed in the territory of former Yugoslavia, in the resolution 771 keeps the option open that such grave breaches are committed in any of the conflicts ongoing at that time. It does not mean that they were, or even could be, committed from a point of view of international law also in the internal Bosnian conflict. The acts in the indictment are prior to the adoption of resolution 780 of 6th October 1992 and resolution 808 of 22nd February 1993 and are, therefore, of little or no relevance. Most of the resolutions to grave breaches, as mentioned by the Prosecution, are adopted later than the period that is covered by the indictment. Resolution 827 asks to provide evidence of the commission of grave breaches and, for practical reasons, is dealing with the whole situation in former Yugoslavia. It has never been contested by the Defence that somewhere in the territory of former Yugoslavia, elsewhere, or perhaps after the time the alleged offences had been committed, the grave breaches provisions might have been applicable. It has correctly been observed by Morris and Scharf that the applicability of the grave breaches provisions in the Croatian conflict did not at all imply that the same was true for the internal Bosnian conflict. I quote: "In this regard, it is necessary to distinguish the Croatian conflict from the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The parties to the Croatian conflict agreed among themselves to apply the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I in their entirety by the Addendum of 23rd May 1992 to the Memorandum of Understanding of 27th November 1991. This agreement to apply to the Croatian conflict, inter alia, the provisions concerning individual criminal responsibility for grave breaches, followed a number of significant event in 1992 including the truce between Croatia and Serbian concluded on 2nd January 1992; Croatia's membership in the United Nations; the proclamation of the New Federal Republic of Yugoslavia consisting of two of the original six Republics as well as Croatia accession to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols thereto. In contrast", Morris and Scharf write, "to the agreement concerning the conflict in Croatia, the special agreement reached on 22nd May 1992 between the parties involved in hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was more limited. It provided for the repression, punishment and prevention of violations of international humanitarian law by the parties but excluded the provisions of the Geneva Conventions concerning individual criminal responsibility." The Security Council, consisting of politicians rather than international lawyers, might well be wrong when they qualify attacks by Serbian Militia -- do they mean Bosnian Serbs -- as violations of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions. The problem here again is that politicians do not care about legal subtleties, and that their legal qualifications of non-specified events -- it is very global -- cannot bind and not even solidly guide the Tribunal in this case. It may be clear, and it has never been contested by the Defence, that the Security Council had in mind that in some respect the grave breaches provisions did apply in the former Yugoslavia. Where the Prosecution argues that grave breaches are by definition acts committed in an international conflict, they seem to have forgotten that they argued before the Trial Chamber that the grave breaches provisions can become operative by special agreements as well. As I just indicated by quoting Morris and Scharf, this may have been the actual situation in the Croatian conflict. The conclusion that the mere attribution of jurisdiction over grave breaches in Article 2 of the Statute indicates that Security Council deemed the conflict to be international is untenable, therefore, and contradictory to what the prosecution has argued before. The Prosecution makes reference to the remark by the Secretary-General that the neutral date chosen for the commencement of jurisdiction is not tied to any specific event, and that it is clearly intended to convey the notion that no judgement as to the international or internal conflict is expressed. Paragraph 61 of the report. The Prosecution, however, rephrases this remark by adding to it that the Secretary-General is not giving a judgement on the character of the conflict on January 1st 1991. That is not what it says, however. The Secretary- General refrains from such judgement without any limitation. Could he not have easily expressed his view to the character of the conflict at the time of the presentation of his report? No, he just does not take a position at all, and leaves it entirely to the Tribunal. I can understand why the Prosecution is very much worried about the issue. It is because it might be difficult to prove that the acts contained in the indictment are related to an international conflict, a the Prosecution would have to do for any of the charges brought against the accused under Article 2 and 3 of the Statute. It would at least be highly inconvenient both for the Prosecution and for the Tribunal, since the Trial Chamber has determined that little of the great volume of material before the Trial Chamber, containing clear indications that the acts alleged in the indictment are committed in the course of an international armed conflict, is such that judicial notice can be taken of it, and none of it is in the form of, nor has it been tendered, as evidence. But inconvenience can never be a prevailing argument when the Tribunal has to decide whether it can exercise jurisdiction over the offences the accused is charged with. It is within the task of the Prosecution to provide evidence for the existence of an international armed conflict. This also seems to have been accepted by the Prosecution where it relies on Rule 94 of the Rules of procedure and evidence. The Defence disagrees, however, with the Prosecution where it argues that the existence of an international armed conflict is a fact of common knowledge. I would not like to insult Mr. Fenrick that he was not even aware of the facts that are of common knowledge at that time. But as argued before, it must be proven that an international armed conflict existed at the place and prior to the period in which the alleged offences were committed. I will now turn to Article 5, crimes against humanity. The Defence has argued before the Trial Chamber that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction over the charges brought under Article 5 of the Statute (crimes against Humanity) because no armed conflict at all existed at all the relevant times and places. Since the debate before the Trial Chamber was very much concentrating on the issue of whether there was an situation of an international or an internal armed conflict, the position of the Defence, a primary argument in relation to Article 5 of the Statute and implicitly a subsidiary argument in relation to the charges brought under Article 2 and 3 of the Statute, might not have caught the attention it needs. The argument has been developed by the Defence during the session of 25th July, pages 104 and 105 of the transcript. I hasten to add to this that the discussion as it can be read in the pages 108 to 113 of the transcript of 26th July may have caused quite some confusion. Therefore, I quote first my colleague Mr. Wladimiroff on what he said on 25th July. He said: "We have as the remaining areas, areas in the control of the Bosnian Serb government with small concentrations of Muslims. That, indeed, was the case in the Opstina of Prijedor. There were, indeed, small concentrations of Muslims in this area. We suggest that in this Opstina the conflict expressed itself in different ways: Armed action by the Bosnian Serb government troops, and conflicts, whether armed or not, ethnically different persons being disorganised or maybe organised or militia of just armed civilians. So we have to distinguish between two groups I repeat that", I am still quoting, "Bosnian Serb government troops taking over in places, in villages, in towns, and on the other hand conflicts, whether armed or not, between persons of different ethnical descent: They were organised, they were not organised, in some parts the militia took a part in it and at other times just armed civilians. We also suggest that the acts of violence which took place there in this Opstina took place entirely within the area under the control of the Bosnian Serb government. There was no control by the Muslim government, no control by the Croat government. It was in the heart of the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb government". The position taken by the Defence before the Trial Chamber was clarified by the example, triggered by Judge Stephen, concerning a hypothetical situation on the Isle Jutland, while the German forces would have invaded the mainland of Denmark. Unfortunately, I must admit, my colleague Mr. Wladimiroff was mixing up the question of whether there was a conflict at all in the Opstina of Prijedor and the question whether this conflict was of an international character. This was, presumably, due to the fact that the motion incorrectly, as I have to admit as well, required the existence -- talking the first motion on jurisdiction -- of an international armed conflict in order to make the jurisdiction under Article 5 of the Statute operative. That was a wrong position. The quoted parts of pages 104 and 105 of the transcript of 25th July make clear, however, that the Defence was, and is of the opinion, that the actual situation in the Opstina of Prijedor showed no armed conflict in the legal technical meaning of this term. Of course, one could doubt as to whether your Honours will address the issue. If you would determine that the position of the Defence has been unclear before the Trial Chamber and that, therefore, the Trial Chamber has rightly understood that it was the position of the Defence, at least, that its position was restricted to the denial of the existence of an international armed conflict in the Opstina of Prijedor, you might consider that the Defence is tariff in clarifying, or even changing, its position now. The rules of procedure and evidence are not clear, as far as I understood them. It is not clear as to whether the parties are allowed to present new -- I would rather say, however, re-phrased or clarified -- elements in their arguments on jurisdiction during the appellate proceedings. It is not clear, as a matter of fact, whether the appellate proceedings are proceedings de Nov day or whether they are just a review of the earlier decision. I will have to accept your decision on this point as it will be. Of course, I do apologise to the extent the confusion has been caused by the Defence. It should be noted, however, that from a point of view of procedural economy, it might be very wise to include the issue in the decision that you will render. As you might know, an amended indictment has been confirmed in this case. If you will not address the issue in your decision (and I have to accept your decision to that extent), the Defence will have to put it forward in a motion on jurisdiction concerning the amended indictment. It has been always intended by the Defence to prevent any unnecessary delay in the proceedings. The Defence has also waited until now to file a motion on jurisdiction concerning the amended indictment until the Appeals Chamber would have rendered its decision. It is useless to find a new motion which is identical to the one the Appeals Chamber has already decided upon, since the outcome will be clearly identical as well. Even if we were to blame for the unclarity and the confusion, however, we would be under an obligation towards our client to raise that issue again, and better, in a new motion on jurisdiction concerning the amended indictment. We, therefore, suggest that you address the issue in your decision, thus probably avoiding a very unattractive and very undesirable delay. I can imagine that you would like to decide upon our suggestion, rather than listening to an expose that is out of order anyhow and after having heard the Prosecution before I proceed on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to dwell on this notion of armed conflict for some time. I read your brief and there you make it clear that you now take a more radical position to the effect that, according to Defence, no armed conflict, as you say, in the legal technical meaning of this term was underway at the appropriate moment in that area. May I ask you a question? What do you mean b "an armed conflict in the legal technical meaning of this term"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will address that issue later on. I have prepared it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you could wait for that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like, as I say, to spend some time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will address the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to say a word on what you have been saying a moment ago, that you felt there might have been some confusion in the presentation of your argument in the first instance, and you were asking yourself, and asking us, whether or not you might not repair this confusion and put your argument today as you think it should have been put originally. I just wanted, Mr. President, to say that personally, I am just giving my personal view on that, I do feel that the Appellant should be allowed to modify or amend his position on that particular point. We are here to render judgement. This is not a cat and mouse game. If you think that your position would be more readily and better presented by changing somewhat your approach, for one, I would be quite prepared to say: "By all means do so," especially since you have then drawn our attention that otherwise you might have to make another motion on jurisdiction which you yourself have qualified as not a very attractive proposition which is a view I do share indeed I suggest that, Mr. President, we should allow the Appellant to put his case as he thinks it should be put now. I am sure that the Prosecutor would not feel aggrieved by this matter in the light of what we have heard as of the moment. That is the suggestion I would wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: There is another view to the matter which my learned brother Judge Deschênes has just referred to. In normal circumstances, the proper procedure would be for you to withdraw the part of the appeal relating to this subject, seeking the permission of the appellate bench that you may raise it again properly before the trial judge, because you have a right to come up again in appeal, notwithstanding the delay that would occur. It would not be correct that we should pre-empt ourselves the right of the trial judge and just start straightaway discussing this matter in appellate jurisdiction with different facts and figures which you never presented before the Trial Chamber. That is just one view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me to just briefly comment on this remark? Of course, we have considered in following this procedure. On the other hand, it is clear to us that the decision of the Trial Chamber will not be affected by -- "misrepresentation" is a big word -- at least this confusion caused by the Defence. I have to think this over, whether we should do this. If you allow me first to proceed and I will think it over during lunch break on whether that would be a more appropriate procedure. If you say: "Think it over first", I have a bit of a problem, I must admit, that the communication with co-counsel at this moment is rather difficult for me; you know the circumstances. So I have to think over things for four persons instead of just myself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Prosecutor whether he would object to your presenting this, I mean, changing your approach and, of course, insisting on this particular point that, according to you, no armed conflict at all existed? Then we may decide at lunch-time and issue an order on this very point. Mr. Prosecutor, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, the approach I would take, with respect, is that in respect of any legal argument in respect of any matters that this Appeal Chamber can take into account, the duty of counsel on both sides is to assist this Chamber, as it would in the case of a Trial Chamber, to come to a just, fair and correct result. We would welcome this Chamber receiving any argument, whether or not it was put before the Trial Chamber. Indeed, I must confess we are doing the same thing. If we were bound, and this Appeal Chamber was bound, it would really be placing itself in a position where it would preclude itself from correcting something that was incorrect. So, we would raise absolutely no objection to the course suggested by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: If I might just add a word? With all due respect, we are sitting here on an appeal which is concerned with the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. B definition, that is a matter which should be decided as a preliminary decision to anything that may happen later on. I think that is an additional ground why we should give this possibility to Appellant as well as to the Prosecutor, if ever necessary, so that we be in a position to envisage the whole of the jurisdictional situation, and decide that once and for all within this piece of litigation. I do not think that it would be in the interest of anyone, and not in the interest of justice, that we put over the decision on this particular point due to a somewhat technical approach to another time, another day and especially after a trial or before another trial judge. So, I suggest that that is an additional reason why we should not hesitate to grant the wish of Appellant's counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I take your point but, as I say, I take the liberty of insisting on my view that we should deliberate on this particular point at lunch-time. We could stop now, if it is convenient for you, and then when we come back at 2.30, when we resume our hearing at 2.30, we will issue an order on this particular point. We have now heard your views and then in the light of this order you might wish to proceed in one way or another. So I suggest that we stand in recess until 2.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you will allow me, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In order to make your scheduling a bit more easy, I can tell you that I had some 45 pages and I have left eight of them, so that is just to give you an indication of how much time 37 pages needed and what I have still prepared on paper. Of course, I cannot say anything about questions you will ask of me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I assume there will be questions this afternoon when we resume after your exposition, so probably you will need one more full hour probably and then we will ask the Prosecutor. We will stand in recess until 2.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, before we start, let me read out our ruling. RULING

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber, having considered the request of the Appellant and heard the Prosecutor, has unanimously decided to grant such request. Both parties are, therefore, free to raise before the Appeals Chamber additional arguments on jurisdiction, even if such arguments had not been presented to the Trial Chamber. You may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may proceed, your Honour, I first would like to give an answer to the question you raised this morning in relation to the definition of Kirgis and the concept of legislation. I have tried to read the article of Kirgis and the far shorter abstract of the article of Yemin -- it is not an Article but it is part of a thesis -- over lunch-time. The first thing, I would like to stress that we are talking about a definition of legislative acts within the very specific setting of the United Nations, although Yemin makes it more broad, the concept. Definition of a legislative process and essential rules that should be valid in the law-making process, are two different things. I think that the law-making process, the legislative process, any Security Council has not been properly defined. But if I look more closely to the elements of the definition, then it seems to me that an executive decree by an omnipotent President, for example, or dictator or whoever would be under this definition a legislative act as well. From a functional point of view, this certainly might be true. But the requirement that a Tribunal should be established by law is interpreted by many (and, as a matter of fact, I have not seen any other interpretation) as a prohibition to create Tribunals by executive orders. Therefore, the functional definition cannot be the final test. Legislation to be valid requires consistency in its temporal and geographical applicability. It requires to create equality. If I take the definition, then it says as the third element, that the legal norm in question is general in nature, that it is directed only to indeterminate addressees and capable of repeated application in time. Then, of course, we come to a very difficult point because all these criteria are relative. If, for example, you would create jurisdiction to try all people that commit violence in the 42nd Street in New York over one year, then you could say that it could be repeated in time, and the addressees are not individualized but are meeting the requirement that they are indeterminate. On the other hand, if you would compare these people to the other inhabitants of New York, then you would say that the addressees are determined. That exactly might be the question in this legislative, if you call it that way, procedure, because you could say it could be repeated in time to the extent that all the war crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia can be subjected to the jurisdiction. On the other hand, you could also say that it is not capable of repeated application in time because it does not cover any conflict that arises tomorrow. So, therefore, it is not capable of being repeated in time. So I think that, first of all, we are dealing with a definition which leaves open the major issues that we have raised. Secondly, because of its functionality, the definition as such is also valid for the kind of legislation which is exactly not covered by the requirement that a Tribunal should be established by law, as it has to be understood in Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the provision in the Inter-American Convention on Human Rights. It is exactly the inconsistency of the Security Council that it makes it unfit to create law as meant in "established by law", these articles. So, from a functional point of view, it might be true but, nevertheless, it is not merely a functional matter. There are also requirements that go further. I think it is most important, especially in the article of Yemin, he point out that this kind of legislation can be made also by executive orders. It is clear from all the commentators and case law on "established by law" that one of the things that especially is forbidden by the requirement "established by law" is that the law is created or the Tribunal is created by executive order. If I may proceed, your Honour, that was my answer to the question you this raised this morning. Having heard your decision on the scope of the appeal, I would rather like to continue with some remarks as to the scope of jurisdiction under Article 5, crimes against humanity and, as I hope, in a proper way now. I repeat, that it is contended by the Defence that no armed conflict at all existed at the relevant time and in the relevant places. It is, therefore, submitted that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction over the charges brought against the defendant under Article 5 of the Statute. One of the consequences, however, would be that the Tribunal would have no jurisdiction either concerning the changes brought under Articles 2 and 3 of the Statute. The Defence has consistently taken the position that the Tribunal should regard the context in which the alleged crimes have taken place (in an armed conflict, in an internal one, in an international one?) on the basis of the geographical variety of the different conflicts going on in the former Yugoslavia. So let me come to the question: What actually happened in the Opstina of Prijedor at the relevant time? At April 30th 1992, the City of Prijedor, the area where Tadic lived, was taken over by the Serbs without violence amounting to an armed conflict. Where in a report of Gow it is stated that there was no meaningful resistance until the take over of Prijedor, the Defence holds that a take over was of a rather administrative character. The Serbs took political and administrative power. When I am talking about "Serbs", I am talking about ethnical Serbs and not about nationals of Serbia Montenegro. This position of the Defence is supported strongly by the findings of the Commission of Experts in its final report on pages 37 to 43 which part specifically deals with the Opstina of Prijedor. The Opstina of Prijedor was an area under control of the Bosnian Serb government. There were at that time still living a small number of Muslims. On May 19th 1992, the Yugoslav National Army (JNA) withdrew from the area. Until then it remained there because, until shortly before, the area was part of the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state did, of course, not cause JNA to vanish immediately, to vanish in the air. But, upon its withdrawal, soon afterwards, part of the JNA military staff and men stayed behind in Bosnia, but they were no longer employed by the JNA. Some of them adhered to the Bosnian Serb Army. In general, one can say that the equipment became available either to the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims armed forces. The logic of some portions of the former JNA to stay behind with equipment is clear if we look at the conclusions in Opinion 9, cited in Opinion 11, of the Arbitration committee, chaired by Mr. Badinter. None of the successor states can claim to be the sole continuing state. It was a process of disintegration wherein every state and/or faction took its part. We suggest that in this Bosnian Serb controlled Opstina, the conflict expressed itself in different ways. Armed action by Bosnian-Serb government troops mainly against civilians and conflicts, whether armed or not, between ethnically different civilians and groups, although being disorganised they never amounted to an armed conflict in its legal technical meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, I have very, very much difficulty in following the reasoning that you are putting before us now. You say there was no armed conflict. Nevertheless, on the one hand, you say there was a JNA army which was there and withdrew. On the other side, there were armed forces that were there and progressed and finally took over Prijedor. Obviously, there was a collision of forces over there. The line to me is very thin between that situation and an armed conflict. I am not sure that because maybe no shots were fired -- I do not know -- this would mean that there was no armed conflict at the time. Really, I am just wondering what is needed to say there is an armed conflict, when I have an army on one side and armed forces on the other side, and one leaving and the other one coming in and taking position. There may have been political negotiations or pressures being exerted but, really, I would need more than what you are telling us now to come to the conclusion that there was no armed conflict at the time and, therefore, we would have no jurisdiction. On that particular point, I need a far more convincing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I do understand that you need more. As a matter of fact, I have a bit more for you. But, to make it clear, I just made an introduction of the happenings before 19th May because the situation changed basically afterwards. I am just explaining, since so many people talk about the presence of the JNA, I am just trying to explain what happened before the period after 25th May because then the JNA left at least to the extent that they became under the control of the Serbian government -- the real Serbian, not the Bosnian-Serb government, but the government of Serbia Montenegro. That is the reason why I explained it, that until that time the JNA was not an external force at that moment, but they were present in the territory of what was at that moment the territory of the state that existed, but as soon as Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent -- I made reference to the report of the Commission Badinter -- they said, well, it was not one state that was remaining and the other, but it was a total disintegration. So, therefore, if you have five areas belonging to one national territory and they divorce in the beginning one national territory, and then it suddenly has to be split up into five, then, of course, you cannot say that the whole army should be put in one of these smaller territories, because one of the conclusions of the Commission Badinter exactly was that there was not one state as the remaining state from the former Yugoslavia, it was a disintegration. So, part of the army went to the Bosnians, part of the army even to the Bosnian-Serbs, Bosnian Croats, etc.. It was a total split-up. So, if we are talking about the presence of JNA staff after 19th May, I would say that they were no longer part of the JNA any more, but because of the disintegration they had become part of the Bosnian-Serb army. What happened after 21st May, I will explain that later. So, I am not neglecting your question, but I have prepared a few more statements on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: I have only one question to ask from you: The application which was filed was for a preliminary motion objection. I do not know what is the position in international law. Will you, please, tell me whether when a preliminary motion is being dealt with by an international court, can we go into mixed questions of law and fact, or only we should go into straight questions of law which are determined by undisputed facts? A question whether an armed conflict took place or not is a mixed question of law and fact until evidence is led on the basis of undisputed documents and witnesses. Can we straightaway give a finding in your favour? No. 2, on a question whether what is the date of the conflict, or what is the time of the offence, whether it should be from January 1991 or, as you put it, April 1991, or May 1992? Again the same question arises: Are we relying on documents which are totally undisputed and from which we must accept as a presumption that what you are stating is true and we then proceed on that basis? This is a question which I want to ask, because I am not used to much exposure on international law, but in the national jurisdiction from which we come, mixed questions of law and fact are not debated in applications for preliminary motion, unless the facts are so obvious and admitted on both sides and there is no dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may answer your question, your Honour? I first want to stress that matters of jurisdiction, as I read in many decisions of the International Court of Justice, are mixed questions as such. What I see that when the ICJ is investigating and deciding upon its own competence, upon its own jurisdiction, then I hope you do not mind at this moment but I have seen several decisions and I remember that it is very clear that they all say that this is such a mixed question, and they deal with it while deciding upon the jurisdiction and before going into the substantive matter of the case. They say: "We have to consider relevant facts for the jurisdiction, perhaps these are not all the facts relevant for the case, but facts relevant for the jurisdiction have to be examined, and the applicable law on these jurisdictional relevant facts has to be established and then we can go into the case". So I do agree with your Honour that it is a mixed question but, as far as I am aware, in the case law of international judicial organs, the question is decided upon mainly at the beginning of the case. Then I think your second question was: What acts are we taking about as to establish the jurisdiction? We have a minor problem in that. First of all, we are not talking about facts only since January 1st 1991, because I concentrate on those acts that Mr. Tadic has been charged with. If you look on the one side at the period described in the indictment in general terms, it seems to be a bit broader than the period of time which is specified for all the relevant facts. I must admit, I cannot reproduce it immediately by heart, but I remember that my colleague Mr. Wladimiroff has paid a lot of attention, especially to this aspect, and this could be found in the transcripts. I would very much like to find the exact places. I could do it, perhaps, during tea break, but if I would do it now it would take about -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I can tell you because I took some notes. According to the Prosecutor, the relevant events occurred between 24th May and 30th August 1992; whereas, according to the Defence, Professor Wladimiroff, page 92 of the transcript, they occurred between 27th May and 3rd August 1992. So you were right in saying -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We noticed that there is a slight difference in the general period, the period of time that is generally described, and the time which is at stake for the individual act. So that is my answer to your question that I am concentrating. Therefore, I have started on 30th April 1992 because that is not yet a start of this period but it comes near then and, therefore, I discussed this part of the events in Opstina of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I put another question? You see, the position is this: It is quite correct that the Prosecution have given a date as regards the offence. The Statute also talks of a date, that from this particular date retrospectively also people who have committed offences can also be tried. What I want to say is please enlighten me -- as I say, I do not know international law and have no exposure as you have -- first, does the ICJ, normally it is exercising civil jurisdiction basically, in civil jurisdiction parties admit facts and documents and they are taken into consideration as admitted facts and documents. In the criminal jurisdiction, is there such a procedure in international law that facts and documents can be admitted by parties and straightaway you proceed, because otherwise you will have to show that all the facts about which you are speaking are undisputed facts, because then you are coming here to answer a question of law. Otherwise, it will be a mixed question of law and fact and I would like to know whether these matters would not ultimately have go to the trial court for proper sifting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me, your Honour, I would first like to make a preliminary remark to your question, and it is that, unlike in civil proceedings, in criminal proceedings it is the task of the Prosecution to prove all relevant facts. If you look at the criminal law, we see that there are different systems operating in the world. I do not know them all but I know a few of them. For example, if you look at the Anglo American systems, you will see that if a defendant expresses a plea of guilt, then the facts, the charges brought by the Prosecution are just accepted in the procedural sense as to be true. There are other systems, however, for example, I do not think that in the Italian system and especially not, for example, the German system, the Dutch system, the French system, that we have a situation where the parties can decide to some extent whether they admit facts or not. For example, in an Anglo American criminal procedure, it might be the case that, although a judge is not convinced at all that the defendant who enters into a plea of guilt is guilty but, nevertheless, for procedural reasons consequences will be drawn out of that. If, on the contrary, in a Continental European system, I would say: "I am guilty", but if there is no evidence according to the law, or if the judge is not convinced that it is true, then he may acquit the person involved. Then, of course, you have several systems such as that entirely the conviction of the judge is decisive; the French express it in the wording "conviction intime" of the judge. But there are other systems. For example, the conviction intime is not a decisive element in Dutch law of procedure; it is not in German procedure either. Sometimes you have very specific rules on what is the minimum of evidence that has to be produced. So, I could not answer this question easily as to how it functions in criminal procedure because there are so many different systems. Of course, I do agree with you that in quite a lot of case law of the ICJ that especially the position parties take in the procedure may be of relevance, even of high relevance, for the establishment of facts. You see, not in all systems but in many systems, that in civil procedures if one party states that fact X happened and if the other party does not deny it, then the court will accept that fact X really has existed. Therefore, it is rather difficult for me to answer your question. On the other hand, it is our position that the Prosecution should establish beyond reasonable doubt that those facts which will make the judicial rules operative did exist. If we are talking facts that are disputed, it is exactly the Defence at this moment who is disputing the facts that have been presented by the Prosecution. As to the question of what kind of documents could be used in evidence etc., the problem, of course, is that rules and procedure in evidence give no clear answer to that, but if I may refer to the -- I am a bit hesitant to do this again and again because I think the situations are not comparable -- decisions of the International Court of Justice, then I see some great reluctance in using whatever documents in order to establish the facts, but very often great weight is given to, for example, consistent statements of official authorities of the state party involved in the conflict, or great weight is given to the position that has been taken by the party in the procedure before the ICJ. You will see that especially it becomes a problem when one of the parties is withdrawing from the procedure in the International Court of Justice. What I am trying do at this moment is to dispute all the facts that have been presented. I am not talking about the form in which they were presented, because the Trial Chamber has been very clear that these documents, that all the material that is available, has not been presented in such a way that judicial notice can be taken. So, I am not specifically addressing this procedural technical issue at this moment, but I am stressing that it is up to the Prosecution to establish these facts relevant for the jurisdiction and I am disputing them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: May I put another question with your kind permission?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: I agree with you that the Prosecution has to prove its case to the hilt. That is the basic position in criminal law. Then you mention you have not read the Rules of the Tribunal or have not been able to make a clear assessment now. What will be the position as regards disputed facts or facts regarding which presumptions should be raised? Once a prime facie case has been proved to the satisfaction of a trial judge, and he issues warrants for arrest, it shows that for the time being the facts which have been presented by the Prosecution are ex facie correct until they will be displaced by you. Will you displace only in arguments in a preliminary objection application? You will have to come to the merits of the case before the trial court. There you will take up the position by seeing what evidence is being led by the other side, how much you can cross-examine them, how much you can dislodge them, dispose of them, and your own evidence. Then there will be some crystallization of the facts. What are the facts now which can be taken as proved? What are the facts which cannot be taken as proved? What are the facts regarding which presumptions can be raised either way? Then we have an assessment. Now, according to you, we should assume everything which the Prosecution has said is not true, but all what you are saying is true; we should assume that there was an armed conflict or no armed conflict at a particular time and place, or that the crimes are of an international character or not character, or do not bear that character without any evidence. It is almost like saying that we accept you now as gospel truth and should decide this case on the basis of your own facts. I do not think that is a correct way of looking at the criminal case. As I said once again, I am only giving this viewpoint from the national point of view, but if you will clarify it from the international point of view, I shall be thankful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, it creates some difficulties for me, your position that you express at this moment. First of all, I made reference to the case law of the International Court of Justice where facts relevant for the establishment of the jurisdiction are decided upon at an early stage. Of course, I can imagine that if the case goes on after the decision on the jurisdiction has been taken to start with, that things might turn out to be a bit different in a later stage when more witnesses have been heard etc. etc. But if there is no jurisdiction, it should be established now because one of the principles of criminal law -- that is, of course, different to the situation in all those cases that have been dealt with by the International Court of Justice. Mr. Tadic is in detention now. If it were to turn out after procedure of one or two years that there would be no jurisdiction, I think we can deal with these facts perhaps a bit more on a global basis in this period of time. You do not have to believe all what I say. I will give you the sources later on, just as the Prosecution has given the sources. I think it is up to the Tribunal to decide to what extent they want to go into these facts, but I think that it is impossible to give a proper decision on jurisdiction if just the facts presented by the Prosecution would be accepted. Of course, if there is a prime facie case , but one of the things I am doing at this moment that the facts presented by the Prosecution can be disputed for very, very good reasons and, therefore, it is submitted to your Tribunal that you should decide on the matter after having established relevant facts, not all relevant facts but those relevant facts, for the decision on jurisdiction. That is my position, but I do understand that you look upon the question differently.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I clarify one point which may seem somewhat obvious? The issue whether or not an armed conflict occurred in that particular area in that particular period relates to jurisdiction, because if no armed conflict occurred, of course, we lack jurisdiction. So, to look into this matter we have to look into facts but, of course, these are facts related on whether or not the armed conflict occurred there, not the allege offences committed by the defendant. We will not pronounce upon that. It is a question of merit on which we cannot pronounce. It is for the Trial Chamber to decide, assuming that we conclude we have jurisdiction, whether or not the offences with which the defendant is charged were actually committed. Therefore, the facts that you will discuss only relate to whether or not an armed conflict occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, therefore, you can proceed and also to give us the sources of your information so that we can compare those sources and decide whether or not we can take judicial notice of some facts or we should look into them. Please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Can I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On this very issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LI
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, your Defence contends that since there was no armed conflict, whether international or national or internal, in the relevant place and time, so the accused is not guilty of any of the crimes charged against him. This is to look at the armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia in isolation without regard to other places and times, without regard to other places of the former Yugoslavia and without reference, without regard to any other time. Do you think that this contention is fair and reasonable in view of the following two facts? The first, fact, the criminal acts of the accused, if proven constitute intentional execution of the policy of ethnic cleansing which has been planned to be executed by force including armed force in most of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and even in Croatia. This is the first fact. The second, it has been reported in mass media that, in fact, the Serbs have occupied about 70 per cent of the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If there has been no attack, no armed attack, in most parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, will the Bosnia-Herzegovina government willingly surrender such a great part of territory to the Serbs? So, for the correct application of international humanitarian law, do you think this Tribunal should not consider the armed conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina and even in Croatia from its commencement up to the present in its entirety, not excluding intervention from outside? Please answer me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to do so, your Honour. I think that, if I understood your question well, the first thing you wanted to know is whether other places and times might be relevant in order to establish whether there was an armed conflict, internal or international. I have to stress that it is clear from the history of the Statute of this Tribunal that at least, as far as the time is concerned, it was the intention of the Security Council that this Tribunal would decide when, and I add to it, where, armed conflicts, either internal or international, existed. I think, as far as the time is concerned, there is no doubt about that, that it was the intention of the Security Council that your Tribunal will have to establish these facts. It would also be difficult to do it in another way, because if we start these proceedings in saying: "Well, there was an international armed conflict anyhow", why, then the whole question of jurisdiction, which it is your task to decide upon it, would be decided already by the press, the Security Council, all those, I would say, forces, organs, institutions, where we were never able to present our view on what happened. So, I think it is a requirement of due process of law that in these proceedings these facts should be established. You say: "Well, it is common knowledge that all criminal acts happened there, there was intentional ethnic cleansing going on at that time". First of all, these are general statements. It is not a matter of whether there was any ethnical cleansing to happen in the territory of former Yugoslavia; it is the question of whether Mr. Tadic can be tried for the acts he is charged with, and if there is jurisdiction to try him, then we would have to establish whether he was guilty of those acts he is charged with, as far as I see, but ethnic cleansing as a form of genocide has not been charged. So, it might be true, it might be horrible. Therefore, I am not used to speak in terms of qualifications. I think one of the basics in a criminal procedure is that you do not charge someone with an offence, you are charging someone to have committed certain behaviour. Once it has been established that it really was the behaviour of the defendant, then you have to find whether this behaviour constitutes an offence or not. So, therefore, I have some difficulties in talking about criminal offences in general terms. I think it should be established in this case whether all the requirements are fulfilled that are necessary to adopt the view that your Tribunal has jurisdiction. Then, of course, we have to establish whether all these facts and details are committed by the defendant or not. The second question I would like to address is your question, you said: "Well, there were so many Serbs on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was this invasion welcomed by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" I am afraid that there is some misunderstanding as to the facts. In 1991, so before the outbreak of the conflict, there were living 47,745 Serbs already on the territory which is now Bosnia-Herzegovina that was at that time already one of the Federal states. So, even if violence was used by Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would say it is almost common knowledge that the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina already for quite many years, and it had nothing do with the conflict, consisted of Serbs, Muslims and Croats. For example, in 1991 there were 47,000 Serbs, 49,000, so almost an equal number, of Muslims and 6,000 Croats. I am citing from the report of the Commission of Experts. So, when we are talking about activities of Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina, I am mainly referring to activities of the local population of Serbian origin. It was not a matter that it invaded the territory o Bosnia-Herzegovina; they lived there already for ages. So I feel that there might be some misunderstanding as to these facts. When I am talking about Serbs, then I will usually be precise whether I mean Serbian Serbs, that means Serbs that were of the Serbian nationality -- Serbia being one of the former Federal states of the former Yugoslavia -- or I am talking about Bosnian Serbs, and then I am referring to citizens of the former Federal state of Bosnia, although they were from Serbian origin. So, if you say: How could it be possible that they came in not welcomed by the government; there must have been violence, etc.? My answer is they were there. They lived there. They still live there. Yes. Of course, I totally agree with you, your Honour, that I will not talk about whether Mr. Tadic was guilty of certain offences or not; I am talking about the situation existing in the Prijedor area because that is the context in which the facts he is charged with have been allegedly committed. One of the last words I spoke before the interruption was that acts of violence which took place there, took place entirely within the area under the control of the Bosnian-Serb government. The global picture of the area I gave is fully in accordance -- I now come to the sources -- with the findings of the Commission of Experts in its final report in 1994. I have some problems, I must say, that we have the final report of the Commission of Experts which has a ver precise paragraph on the Opstina of Prijedor, but all the annexes to the report where detailed information is given exactly about the investigation that was held in Prijedor is, unfortunately, not released. If we look at the annexes -- they are United Nations documents -- all the annexes are published apart from annex 5 which is called the Prijedor Report. One of my problems is that the Prosecution, as is known to me, has available this annex which gives precise and detailed information, and since I will talk about the general part of the report later on, there might be a necessity to check in the annex whether it is a good summary of the findings of the Commission as they are contained in the annex. So, that is a problem for us when we are talking about sources. I will come to that later. I come now to the issues that have been already part of the questions. What is the definition of an armed conflict? I would like to refer to the definition in Article 1.1 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions. Although it is not perhaps relevant or applicable in this case, I think for the matter of finding what is an armed conflict it might be relevant. What is an armed conflict? That is, "... all armed conflicts which are not covered by Article 1 of Protocol I and which take place in the territory of a High Contracting Party between its armed forces and dissident armed forces or other organised armed groups which, under responsible command, exercise such control over a part of its territory as to enable them to carry out sustained an concerted military operations and to implement this Protocol. The Protocol shall not apply to situations of internal disturbances and tensions, such as riots, isolated and sporadic acts of violence and other acts of a similar nature, as not being armed conflicts ...". Therefore, if you look at the definition, since no armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia -- then I am talking about what I would say the official, the Muslim republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- were involved in the violence going on in the Bosnian controlled area of the Opstina of Prijedor, and since none of the other groups or individuals involved qualify either as dissident armed forces or other organised armed groups meeting the requirements of the definition of Protocol II, there was no armed conflict going on in that area. I do not say there was no violence but, as a matter of fact, these acts of violence were clashes among the different members or smaller armed groups of the population within the Bosnian Serb controlled area of the Opstina. The actions of the Bosnian Serb army were not directed against, nor did they affect, the armed forces of the internationally recognised state, Bosnia-Herzegovina, on whose territory the violence took place. As I told you before, one of the requirements is that the violence, that the conflict, must be between the armed forces of the High Contracted Party, so that is the recognised state, and other groups. So, the Bosnian Serb army, since the Republic Srpske was not a recognised state and was not a party to the Convention, cannot be regarded as this central army against which there should be some fighting. Even if one would argue, however, that the ongoing armed conflict in other areas of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina caused the existence of a relevant internal conflict (between Muslim Bosnians, Bosnian Croats and Serbian Croats), then it should be observed that no nexus can be established between the internal conflict, internal conflict between the different groups, and the acts the defendant is charged with. The same would be true, as a matter of fact, if one would accept that an international armed conflict was existing at the time and place relevant for the indictment because the nexus is missing. The nexus required may not derive as a necessary element from customary law as such, but the nexus that the acts have to be committed in armed conflict is clearly expressed in Article 5 of the Statute. What does this mean, that the acts are committed "in" an armed conflict? James O'Brien has given a just interpretation of this requirement in writing. I quote: "A reasonable approach is to interpret 'in' armed conflict in accordance with the restrictive language of the Nuremberg Charter for preconflict acts: They must be shown to have been committed in execution of or in connection with a violation of the laws of armed conflict or genocide." I continue quoting: "It may seem odd to interpret 'in' as meaning both 'during' and 'in execution of or in connection with'. However, a change in a material fact the start of the conflict, justifies the dual construction. Furthermore, this approach respects the plain language of the Statute (which requires that crimes against humanity be 'committed in armed conflict' even while extending that jurisdiction to January 1st 1991, before many would acknowledge the existence of armed conflict)." The position of the Defence on this issue is again in line with the findings of the Commission of Experts in its final report. The Commission cannot conclude that the events in the Prijedor area qualify as either grave breaches or as war crimes. This is quite understandable if you appreciate that the events are described by the Commission as not taking place in an armed conflict, let alone in an international armed conflict. The Commission of Experts finds further that it is likely to be confirmed in court under due process of law that these events ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina constitute genocide. So, I am not saying that there were no crimes, but genocide is not one of the crimes that Mr. Tadic is charged with. This is logical in the context of the report as well, since no armed conflict at all is required for the commission of genocide. The Commission holds that it is unquestionable that the events in Prijedor since 30th April 1992 qualify, however, as crimes against humanity. This finding may be acceptable in general terms for the Defence, but is irrelevant, because crimes against humanity under customary international law may be committed without the existence of an armed conflict at all, without the existence of any link between the acts and the armed conflict. The Defence interprets the findings of the Commission of Experts in this way. This leaves alone, however, that Article 5 of the Statute does not invest the Tribunal with jurisdiction over crimes against humanity in general terms, but only if committed in an armed conflict. The Defence would have liked to be able not just to invoke the final report of the Commission of Experts, but also the annexes thereto. One of them exclusively deals with the Prijedor investigation but, unfortunately, this is the one and only annex that has not been published, as I just explained to you. This annex could demonstrate more clearly, as the Defence is informed by sources, that this annex could demonstrate that no armed conflict was going on in the Opstina of Prijedor at the relevant time and, at least, the conclusions in the short final report give rise to the acceptability of this point of view. The Defence, moreover, is rather unhappy with the fact -- I only discussed it this morning with the Prosecution -- that the Prosecution is in the possession of the annex dealing with the Prijedor area. Therefore, the Defence submits that this creates a substantive violation of the principle of equality of arms and, submits that either one or more of the members of the Commission of Experts should be called to give evidence on this issue, or, and that might be perhaps the more easy way at this moment -- I discussed the matter this morning with the Prosecution -- that the annex would be produce or, at least, made available to the Defence as to clarify especially this issue. I gradually came already to a matter of evidence. I would like to make a few final remarks on that. As to the existence of an international armed conflict, the Prosecution has argued that this is common knowledge. As I have demonstrated, both by referring to the authors that deal with this question and to the findings of the Commission of Experts, this is an untenable position and, at least, shows no prime facie case in this respect. Several decisions of the ICJ have been invoked by the Prosecution to support their submissions that the sources available to the Trial Chamber constitute enough evidence as to the questions in relation with the existence of an international armed conflict. I point out that decisive elements of these decisions fail to exist in this case. Since state were parties in these proceedings, they were confronted in the decisions of the ICJ either with consistent statements of their state officials, with the positions they had taken in the proceedings itself, especially when they did not deny the claims of the other parties concerning the facts, or did not at all comment on these claims. Only under these circumstances, where a lot of material was available on events that appeared in the headlines of all the world's newspapers, the Court was willing to take notice of that material. Such a situation -- I repeat it -- does not exist here. In criminal cases, moreover, rules on admissibility of evidence have to be interpreted in a rather formal way and have to be observed very strictly. This is especially true where the events in the Opstina of Prijedor were not the main issue of publication, the press publications, but, rather, the global events going on in Bosnia and in the former Yugoslavia. Finally, this information lacks the necessary precision. That is the reason why I think that the report of Gow but, as I hope even more, the annex to the final report of the Commission of Experts will give proper information as to form at least a provisional opinion on the issue. It is submitted by the Defence that it cannot be established that acts, committed by the defendant and charged under Article 5 of the Statute, were committed in execution of or in connection with an armed conflict. It is also submitted that the required nexus with an armed conflict fails to exist for the acts the defendant is charged with under Article 213 of the Statute, in case the Appeals Chamber would either determine that an international conflict existed at the time and place relevant to the indictment, or that the classification of the conflict is irrelevant. These were my remarks, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to comment on two points, one point of fact and a point of law? A point of fact relates -- actually I myself read the final report of the Commission of Experts, I do not know the annex 5 you mentioned, and -- there is a section on what happened in the Opstina Prijedor.
