utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you look up the relevant paragraphs, in particular, paragraph 163 through 167, you will find a few remarks on which I would like you to comment. May I read out and quote, say, for instance, paragraph 165, which relates to a period you regard as coming within the purview of the scope of events at issue. This is 165, I read out: "On 30th May 1992, a group of less than 150 armed non-Serbs had made their way to the old town in Prijedor to regain control over the town. They were defeated and the old town was razed. In the central parts of Prijedor town, all non-Serbs were forced to leave the houses as Serbian military, paramilitary, police and civilians advanced street by street with tanks and lighter arms. The non-Serbs had been instructed over the radio to hang a white piece of cloth on their homes to signal surrender." I could go on quoting. I wonder if you regard these facts as undisputed, and if these facts could show that actually there was some sort of armed conflict going on on that day, on 30th May 1992, in that particular area. Moving to a point of law, let me ask you whether you could again comment on the facts that I am sure you are aware of, that the definition of armed conflict laid down in Protocol II, Article 1, actually is a very strict definition which was not regarded by many participants in the Geneva Diplomatic Conference as in a way affecting the much broader definition of internal armed conflict laid down in common Article 3 to the four Geneva Conventions. I remember that the representative of the German Democratic Republic, as it was then called, put forward a proposal to this effect, so as to imply that from that moment onwards the definition laid down in Article 1 of Protocol II should in a way be binding also on the parties to the Geneva Conventions, namely, should also effect the much broader definition. This proposal, to the best of my recollection, was rejected. So, as I say, if we now look for a definition of internal armed conflict, it is not sufficient for us just to read what is stated in Article 1 of Protocol II; we should also look at the much broader definition of Article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions. I wonder whether you could comment on this point. Of course, that definition implies that whenever you have any sort of fighting or clashes between the central authorities of a particular country and factions there, or even clashes between two groups, organised groups, of people within the territory of a sovereign state, then you can say that we are confronted with an internal armed conflict. I wonder whether you could comment on this much broader definition of internal armed conflict? I would like to add also that I would welcome your comments on the fact that you may have on this view, namely, you may have an armed conflict, internal armed conflict, even if in one particular area of the territory of the state where the internal armed conflict is underway there is no armed clash; I mean, there is just, as you said, takeover of administrative character. You said -- I took notes -- the Serbs took over control without violence. So, you see, I wonder whether you would regard the armed conflict as taking place only in those particular areas of the territory of a sovereign State where clashes occur, or whether this armed conflict can also in a way extend to areas where there is no resistance, no armed clashes. Actually, this is in a way very clear, if you read common Article 2 to the four Geneva Conventions, where it is stated and I quote: "This Convention shall apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a High Contracting Party even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance." Of course, now we are here within the framework of international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Previously, I was speaking of internal armed conflict. But here again, you see, international law does not require -- this is a question I am asking you. From a quick reading of this provision, one might be led to believe that international does not require armed resistance or clashes between two powers or two organised groups for there being an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would suggest to you that I address the issue and answer your question in the next round, because I am fully aware that any interpretation of paragraph 165 and, of course, it would be in my line of reasoning in saying that they are not holding certain territory, they are not organised, etc. etc., but the two questions are heavily interrelated. Therefore, if you do not mind, I am younger of age and have not been a professional in international law for many years, so I would rather do some homework first and address the issue tomorrow in the afternoon

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: I want to add a footnote so that you would take it into consideration in your answer tomorrow. I had intended to draw your attention to the same point that the President had done and, in fact, I would like to draw your attention to a sentence in Article 1, paragraph 1, of Protocol II which you have cited which I am citing from memory, which says: "The Present Protocol complements the provisions of Article 3 common to the four Conventions without affecting or changing the condition of its application." So that was really intended to say that the conditions of application of Article 3 which are different would continue to exist, but this is simply for your comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you through with your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could take a break now and adjourn and resume at quarter past 4? So we stand in recess until quarter past 4.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you will have seen and read from our brief, we support the conclusions and order that was issued by the Trial Chamber. As indicated in our brief, we also submit that the first two attacks of the Defence which were dealt with today by Mr. Orie, which are aimed at the legality of this Tribunal are not, in our submission, strictly matters relating to jurisdiction, as that word was used in Rule 72(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. You will have also seen, your Honours, that we persist in the attitude taken before the trial court, that this Tribunal has no judicial review power in respect of a decision taken by the Security Council. That having been said, the trial court considered it appropriate to comment. Although it found in favour of that submission with regard to review power, it decided to comment on the submissions put forward on behalf of the Defence, and that too may be the approach taken by this Appeal Chamber with regard to both the question of appealability and the question of reviewability. To the extent that we can be helpful in that regard, I need hardly state that we would be happy to assist to the extent that we can, but our approach in our brief, and the approach subject to any questions from the bench, will be to dwell on the matter which we submit is truly appealable, and that is the question of subject matter jurisdiction. Before I get there, however, if I might deal with two preliminary matters. The one relates to Annex 5 to which Mr. Orie referred earlier this afternoon. I was surprised to hear that he had a problem getting Annex 5 because my understanding was that all the annexes to the Commission of Experts final report had been published as official United Nations documents. During the last adjournment I spoke to Legal Counsel of the United Nations Mr. Corell and he informed me that indeed my understanding was correct and all the annexes, including annex 5, have been published under the reference number S/1994/674 AWD2 an are obtainable on order from the United Nations. So it is open to Mr. Orie to obtain annex 5. If we can be of assistance, and if he would prefer us to obtain it for him, obviously we would be more than happy to do that. But we were not aware until it was raised earlier today that there was any problem on the part of the Defence in obtaining Annex 5. There should be no problem in correcting any disability that there may be in that regard. The second matter, your Honours, is the question that was raised very pertinently by His Honour Judge Sidhwa with regard, if I might broadly refer to it as judicial notice. As he put to Mr. Orie, in national systems judicial notice is a very common and very important tool to avoid unnecessary inconvenience and waste of time with regard to the proof of generally notorious matters. From the few comparative law books available to us, it would appear clear that the judicial notice is something which exists in both the civil and common law systems. Wigmore, the leading Anglo-American author on evidence (paragraph 2571 in the 9th edition) says that judicially noticed facts fall into three categories: Firstly, matters which are actually so notorious that to all, the production of evidence would be unnecessary. Secondly, matters which the judicial function supposes the judges to be acquainted with, in theory at least. Thirdly, sundry matters not included under either of these heads, though are subject for the most part to the consideration that though they are neither actually notorious nor bound to be judicially known, yet they would be capable of such instant an unquestionable demonstration if desired that no party would think of imposing a falsity on the Tribunal in the face of an intelligent adversary." Those are the three categories Wigmore talks about. With regard to the civil law in Capeletti and Perello on Italian law, they state: "In reaching its decision, the court may not rely on its private knowledge. However the court is permitted to take judicial notice of notorious facts and of rules based on common experience. Notorious facts need not be personally known to the court, but must be indisputable and easily ascertainable." Your Honours and your colleagues in framing the Rules of Procedure and Evidence were cognizant of the question of judicial notice, and it was dealt with in Rule 94 which provides that: “A Trial Chamber shall not require proof of facts of common knowledge but shall take judicial knowledge [sic] thereof”. That rule is applicable, by reason of Rule 107 I think it is, to appeal. Rule 107 provides that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that govern proceedings in a Trial Chamber shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to proceedings in the Appeals Chamber. So your Honours are in the same position as the Trial Chamber with regard to preliminary motions and the recognition of judicial notice. The question was raised by his Honour Judge Sidhwa with regard to the question of judicial notice in the international law field. The International Court of Justice has dealt with this question in a number of judgements. It was usefully stated by a Judge Shahabuddeen in the case concerning the application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in 1993, where the learned judge said, when he was dealing with the categories of material admissible in evidence or the principles by which evidence is assessed by ICJ, that: "As regards these, there are no technical rules, such as those which exist in most domestic systems. Referring to the common law best evidence rule, Judge Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice pointedly observed that international tribunals are not tied by such firm rules. Many of them are not appropriate to litigation between governments." There is a caveat there which I would urge notice be taken of. It may be, and we would suggest that it is, necessary for this Tribunal as a criminal tribunal to be perhaps more conservative with regard to judicial notice in a criminal tribunal than the ICJ might be with regard to civil litigation between governments. Governments can look after themselves a lot more easily than accused who appear in criminal courts. Nevertheless, we would submit that this Tribunal should take the judicial notice that it considers appropriate to an International Criminal Tribunal that has been set up specifically for the former Yugoslavia. In other words, it would not take judicial notice in the same way as a court sitting in a Netherlands national court would take sitting in The Hague. This is an international court sitting in The Hague consisting of judges from 11 jurisdictions. We would submit that it must in the interest of fairness and justice take judicial notice of facts which it regards as notorious in the context which it is adjudicating, and that is in the context of the former Yugoslavia. In addition, for example, we would suggest that certainly this court can for certain purposes take notice of United Nations documents. It is an organ of the United Nations. It can certainly, we would submit, take notice of resolutions of the Security Council; of statements made by the President of the Security Council; of officials documents issued by the United Nations. Having referred to official documents of the United Nations, not the same notice can be taken of all contents of documents issued by the United Nations. Facts referred to in the Commission of Experts reports, for example, unless accepted as common cause in a particular case, would be subject to proof. Statements made by the Commission of Experts on legal matters, we would submit, can be taken notice of in the same way as the writings in any textbook could be taken notice of. So it is difficult to be more precise. We would generally submit that one can have regard to the approach in the International Court of Justice, subject to the caveat which I have mentioned. For example, in the Military and Paramilitary Activities judgement in the International Court at paragraph 72 (that is the ICJ Reports 1986, page 44), it was stated: "The court considers that in its quest for the truth it may also take note of statements of representatives of the parties or of other states in international organisations, as well as the resolutions adopted or discussed by such organisations in so far as factually relevant, whether or not such material has been drawn to its attention by a party." S it is a very wide use of judicial notice. In the Nuclear Tests case judgement there was reference to facts in the public domain that the court would take notice of. In this interlocutory appeal we would ask the court, and we have in the appeal brief, to take notice particularly of Security Council resolutions and other notorious state acts which were affected by parties, states in the former Yugoslavia at the relevant time. These are set out in our brief. We would respectfully support the broader approach of the Trial Chamber in not having regard to all of the facts that were presented by both of the parties as having been proven where they are subject to proof. Again in answer to the query put to our learned opponent by his Honour Judge Sidhwa, it would not be proper to deal with the preliminary motion on facts which are disputed, on facts which are not notorious. To the extent that they need to be proved, that is a matter for the Trial Chamber and not a matter fit for preliminary motion. To the extent that the Defence relies on those facts, the preliminary motion must fail. It does not mean that the Prosecutor will not have the burden of proof at the trial, but by the same token it certainly does not mean that the Defence can simply, as it were, by way of preliminary motion put in dispute facts which require proof at a trial. With those preliminary submissions, Mr. President, I will move to deal with the question of subject matter jurisdiction

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, before you move into the substance of your argument, at the very beginning of your remarks you said that you were supporting the conclusion of the trial court as to the fact that this Tribunal has no power of review over the decisions of the Security Council, which is the position actually, I understand, you had taken and argued. I have some trouble with that position, and just before you leave the topic I would like to be, if I may say, reassured. It seems to me that merely as a matter of definition a Tribunal has an inherent power to look over its own powers, its own origin as a matter of fact, and also over its own jurisdiction. That is true both at the international and at the national levels. This would apparently imply that the Tribunal would look at the instruments by which it has been set up and, therefore, examine the "legality" of the position that the Tribunal is in and of the channels through which it has come into existence. This would be a power of review and actually it would be over the decisions of the Security Council. I know that if we were to assert that power that would lead us into unchartered waters. I do not say that we should or we should not, but at the moment of speaking I have some difficulty in convincing myself that sitting here as a member of the Tribunal I and my colleagues should become blind to the origin of the Tribunal, and not be concerned with the events that have led to our sitting here today. I am wondering whether there is a forceful enough argument that we can say, indeed, we have no power of review and that is the end of it. As I say, I am somewhat troubled by that. This does not mean that if we have the power to review we would come to any other conclusion than the one of the trial court, but I would not wish, it seems to me, to be in a position where I am bound not to look into the legality or validity of the steps that have been taken to bring this Tribunal into action. That is exactly one of the arguments that has been raised by the Appellant. I am not sure we should tell the appellant: "Sorry, sir, but we cannot look into your argument."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can think of no national situation where a court created by parliament or by a legislator or by a president having the power, by a sovereign, has the power to question its own legality. The power of judicial review, as it is normally known in national situations, is a power to review statutes of the legislator in most cases which offend the constitution, which is really the ”Grundnorm”, that it can consider its own legality in any respect. That would be the position in a national situation and if it were not so one would lead, inevitably, to the vicious circle that Mr. Orie referred to (was pushed into referring to with respect), and that is the very concept of looking into one's own legality assumes that one has the legality to look into one's own legality. If one finds that one is illegally established, then on what basis does one give a judgement even on that? Mr. Orie suggested in that sort of situation, I suppose, the sensible thing to do is not to deliver a judgement and pack one's bags. That is the difficult vicious circle situation into which one is forced. The reason is not hard to find. It is really that this Tribunal is expressly in terms of the law (by "law" I mean the Charter of the United Nations, which incidentally is a treaty, is treaty law and which the members of the United Nations agreed to be bound by that Charter), in terms of the Charter this is a sub-organ of the Security Council. It would indeed be strange for a sub-organ to question the act done by its creator, in this case the Security Council. We submit it is on that basis that this Tribunal, in our respectful submission, does not have that power to consider its own legality. This was really, as I understand it, the approach of the Trial Chamber. I can do no more than perhaps restate it in different words which I have attempted to do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I can follow up on the question put by Judge Deschênes. If what you just said is correct, how would you comment upon Article 24 paragraph 2 of the UN Charter which I will read out: "In discharging these duties the Security Council shall act in accordance with the purposes and principles of the UN. The specific powers granted to the Security Council for the discharge of these duties are laid down in Chapters VI, VII, VIII and XII." In a way here the UN charter which, as you rightly pointed out, is a treaty and at the same time it is the constitution of the world organisation, set out the sort of parameters or yardstick by which one could claim even the action by the Security Council should be gauged. Ho would you interpret this Article 24, paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Clearly, Mr. President, in terms of Article 24 subparagraph 2, paragraph 2 circumscribes to an extent the powers of the Security Council. The question is whether if it exceeds those powers, a sub-organ of the Security Council is a body which has the power to say so. The International Court of Justice, certainly as I understand the relevant judgement, came to the conclusion that it cannot review the decisions taken by the Security Council. The question is whether this Tribunal is entitled to exercise wider powers in this regard than the International Court itself. The answer really is that it is a matter for the members of the United Nations to keep its own orders in check, and not for any organ of equal status, as is the International Court of Justice, and a fortiori not a sub-organ created by one of the organs itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ABI-SAAB
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, without prejudice to your interpretation of the attitude of the International Court, we may agree or not on that, I want to put a question from another point of view. It is true that the Security Council has established this Tribunal as a subsidiary organ, but it has created a subsidiary organ of a special nature which by its very nature has to act at an arm's length of its creator. If it is a simple subsidiary organ it can take instructions from the parent organ. Obviously this is not so for a Tribunal. A Tribunal has to act as a Tribunal, possessed with a judicial function which demands independence, autonomy, fairness etc. As a judicial organ, at least on the international level, because the examples you gave were basically internal, there is a general principle, I would say that it is common knowledge, which is called “compétence de la compétence”, that the Tribunal is possessed of an inherent power to decide on its own jurisdiction and, as such, to take all pleas to its jurisdiction. Of course, our Tribunal cannot take -- I cannot find the word in English -- “par voie d'action” as a basis of its principal jurisdiction the review of the Security Council, the exercise of its powers, but here the plea is really to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, that if the Tribunal is unconstitutionally constituted it cannot act as a Tribunal. So it is not exactly the same thing as if the Tribunal acts as a constitutional tribunal judging the acts of the Security Council. It simply examines its own legality. Would you put the two the situations on the same level?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that they are on the same level because it is really doing the same thing, and that is second guessing or sitting in judgement over a decision deliberately taken and expressly taken by the body that created the Tribunal. I can do no better than repeat the submission made by Mr. Niemann before the Trial Court, that if for example (and many examples were debated to and fro before the Tribunal Chamber as appears from the transcript) it was a conclusion that the Judges of this Tribunal came to that there was some defect in the Statute which would preclude them from giving a fair trial to persons accused before them, that would not entitle the Tribunal, in our respectful submission, to put right what the Security Council on the hypothetical example got wrong. It would properly from a moral and conscious point of view stand back and say: We cannot do our work in terms of international justice with the Statute in the form in which it is, and we are going to suspend our work and give the Security Council an opportunity of getting it right. That would be the honourable way, in my submission, of dealing with it. If it has the power of review it really opens a floodgate because where does it stop? Does the power of the view in looking at Article 24 include, and must include if one were to follow this argument to its logical conclusion, what are political decisions taken by the Security Council, in this case unanimously but that is very much by the way, in addition to any judicial decisions taken by the Security Council? To an extent the Security Council did legislate. The Statute under which this Tribunal operates is legislation. It clearly did not legislate the international law and it expressly refrained from doing that, with respect wisely. It did not legislate the law, but it certainly legislated in creating and conferring powers on this Tribunal. Whether there is a power of review must be found in the Statute or in other norms of international law. In our submission, there is no norm of international law which would give a sub-organ, even a judicial criminal sub-organ, a right of review over the body which created it. I am not sure I can helpfully take it further than that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Supposing we did not touch this question of ultimately finding that we have to review judicially the resolutions of the Security Council. I want to know as an opinion from you whether as an international criminal jurisdiction created by the Supreme Court at its own highest level, with impartial judges, protection being given to the accused, all the core elements of various human rights law and humanitarian law having been taken into consideration, can it not say that I have looked into my paternity and find legitimacy? Supposing it was otherwise, could I not say that there appears to be some error or mistake, or that the purposes and principles of the Charter have not been complied with, but leave it at that then, no more no less, without then going and saying: "We disband ourselves, we are packing up" or something, telling everybody to go home and leave it to the Security Council or the General Assembly to take such action which they consider is proper in the circumstances without any direction or any recommendation. I think in the Namibia case also one of the judges, I think de Castro, mentioned that we would not co-operate with the legislation if it was illegal. He also left it at that in very genteel language. Can we become gentlemen of that category and be in good company with the ICJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour I would suggest that it was really for these reasons that the Trial Chamber, no doubt, saw fit to deal with the substantive arguments relating to legality. One is left certainly in sitting in an international criminal court with a feeling of unhappiness, and perhaps even frustration, at simply as it was put by one of your Honours, simply closing one's eyes to what on the hypothesis as put to me would be an illegality created by the Security Council. The submission is not that the judges should walk away, but should draw any defect to Security Council, to United Nations and particularly the Security Council, and tell them if they want the independent judges who have been appointed by the United Nations to do their work, they are only prepared to do it on a proper basis and if it can be put right it must be put right. If it is a fundamental defect that cannot be put right, then there would be no point even in doing that, so it would depend very much on the sort of defect it is. Assuming as a hypothesis that this International Tribunal had been given the power to impose a death sentence. It would not be open for this Tribunal, we would submit, to say, well, in terms of current contemporary standards and civilised nations, this is something that is not known and to refuse to do it. Presumably judges who were appointed in those circumstances, if they had a conscientious objection to anything in the Statute, should refuse appointment. If having taken appointment, it is something that can be put right, that should be drawn to the attention of the body that created the Tribunal in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: We have been given paternity without affiliation; we are independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can get then to the question of subject matter jurisdiction. For your convenience, I am sorry to add to the already voluminous papers, w have prepared (I want to refer to number of the resolutions) in a separate volume the resolutions in chronological sequence. It is rather inconvenient in the documents before you the resolutions are in no chronological sequence at all, and one has to go from document 4 to document 27. We thought it would be more convenient, and I would ask if they have not already been given to you that they be ..., here they are. [Handed] There are volumes for each of the members of the bench and also for Mr. Orie. The first submission I would make, your Honours, is that over the years, over many years, the Security Council when passing resolutions on international humanitarian law in particular has made implicit rather than explicit determinations concerning the nature of the conflicts under consideration by it. The fact that such determinations have been implicit in no way, we suggest, detracts from the fact that they were made. In other words, if one finds that an implicit determination has been made by the Security Council or by any other body having power, the fact that it is implicit does not weaken it in any way. One can say things implicitly or explicitly. If as a fact you find it has been said implicitly that makes it, nonetheless, an act by the Security Council or a fact. We start in our brief, and I would start there, with the position and the attitude taken by the Security Council with regard to Israel and the occupied territories, and particularly the position of Jerusalem. After the six-day war in 1967 the government of Israel regarded Jerusalem, the whole City of Jerusalem, a having been reunited and as part of the State of Israel and it regarded its laws as being automatically effective in the whole City and it exercised jurisdiction accordingly. Over many, many years the Security Council has passed resolutions going the other way. If I might refer to the resolution which is No. 3 in the new bundle, resolution 471 of 1980. There the Security Council said on 5th June 1980: "Regarding once again the Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War of 12th August 1949, and in particular Article 27 which deals with protected persons", and they set out the relevant portions of Article 27. They go on to say: "Reaffirming the applicability of the Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War to the Arab territories occupied by Israel since 1967, including Jerusalem." It nowhere says that the laws of international conflict apply either to the occupied territories or to Jerusalem. It is implicitly saying so in the clearest terms by referring to Article 27 which only applies to international conflicts. That is the starting point. It did the same thing, as another example, in resolution 607 which is No. 6 in this bundle. It again reaffirmed the Geneva Convention to Jerusalem some eight years later in 1988. One finds an equivalent approach by the Security Council with regard to Iraq and Kuwait. The invasion of Kuwait by Iraq was regarded by Iraq as an internal matter. It regarded Kuwait as a province or as a part of Iraq, and i objected to this being regarded as an international conflict rather than an internal conflict. How did the Security Council deal with it? In resolution 664 of 1990 the Council started off by demanding that Iraq facilitate the immediate departure from Kuwait and Iraq of nationals of Third Countries. It did not make any explicit determination of international conflict. Its very reference to Third Countries clearly indicated that this was regarded not as an internal conflict, but one in which Third Countries were involved. Resolution 666, which is No. 8 in the bundle, is of particular relevance to this case before the Appeals Chamber. At the bottom of page 22 in the bundle the Security Council said that it was “deeply concerned that Iraq has failed to comply with its obligations under Security Council resolution 664 in respect of the safety and well-being of Third state nationals, and reaffirming that Iraq retains full responsibility in this regard under international humanitarian law, including, where applicable, Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilians in Time of War." Paragraph 2 is of significance: "Expects Iraq to comply with its obligations under 664 in respect of Third State nationals and reaffirms that Iraq remains fully responsible for their safety and well-being in accordance with international humanitarian law, including, where applicable, the Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War." Again no explicit reference to the fact that this was regarded by the Security Council as an international armed conflict. Finally with regard to Iraq and Kuwait, paragraph 13 of resolution 670 which appears No. 9 in the bundle on the second page, in paragraph 13 the Security Council says: "It reaffirmed that the Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War [the Fourth Convention] applies to Kuwait, and that as a high contracting party to the Convention Iraq is bound to comply fully with all its terms and, in particular, is liable under the Convention in respect of the grave breaches committed by it, as are individuals who commit or order the commission of grave breaches." One sees here what I would respectfully submit is almost a code language used by the Security Council. When it refers to "grave breaches" it is clearly, albeit implicitly but nevertheless very clearly, determining and has determined that an international conflict exists. If it did not, clearly the reference to "grave breaches" would be quite inappropriate and we suggest it was very deliberate in this and in the resolutions that applied to the former Yugoslavia. One contrasts with Israel and Jerusalem, and Kuwait and Iraq, the position in the manner in which the resolutions were framed with regard to Rwanda. There the Security Council was clearly dealing with an internal armed conflict. That that was the case again was not stated. There is no resolution of the Security Council dealing with Rwanda which states anywhere that it was dealing with an internal conflict, any more than there was any reference in any of the resolutions of the Security Council to the best of our researches stating that there was an international armed conflict in other situations. It is done implicitly. In resolution 925 of 1994, which is No. 28 in the bundle, I will not quote from it, the Council referred to the commission of genocide in Rwanda. Again, without referring to whether it was internal or international, its reference to genocide was appropriate because that is a crime which can be committed in times of war and peace and certainly in an internal armed conflict. In resolution 935, which is at No. 29, the Security Council established the Commission of Experts for Rwanda. It is instructive to compare the wording of that resolution with the equivalent or similar resolution establishing the Commission of Experts for the former Yugoslavia. In the relevant passage at the top of the second page of 935, the Security Council said: "Recalling that all persons who commit or authorise the commission of serious violations" -- no reference to "grave breaches" as one would expect -- "of international humanitarian law are individually responsible for those violations and should be brought to justice. Requests the Secretary-General to establish as a matter of urgency an impartial Commission of Experts to examine and analyse information submitted pursuant to the present resolution, together with such further information as the Commission of Experts may obtain through its own investigation or the efforts of other persons or bodies, including the information made available by the special rapporteur for Rwanda, with view to providing the Security Council with its conclusions on the evidence of grave violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of Rwanda, including the evidence of possible acts of genocide." If one compares resolution 780 of 6th October 1992, which is at No. 16 in the bundle, one finds almost the same wording with certain important differences. Firstly, the paragraph at the foot of the page the Security Council, expressing once again its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring within the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including reports of mass killings and the continuance of the practice of ethnic cleansing, and then the equivalent paragraph 2: "Requests the Secretary- General to establish as a matter of urgency" the same wording "an impartial Commission of Experts to examine and analyse the information submitted pursuant to resolution 771 and the present resolution, together with such further information as the Commission of Experts may obtain through its own investigations or efforts of other persons of bodies pursuant to 771, with a view to providing the Secretary-General with his conclusions", and here come the different words: "on the evidence of grave breaches of the Geneva Convention and other violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." So again no explicit finding in either case of internal or international, but a very clear implicit determination which is the only possible explanation of the relevant portions of the resolutions to which I have referred. Still dealing with Rwanda, the Security Council itself drafted the Statute for the International Tribunal for Rwanda. That appears from paragraph 9 of the report of the Secretary-General which appears as document No. 31 in the new bundle. The Secretary-General states that the Statute was drafted by the original sponsors of the Security Council resolution 955, and discussed among members of the Council. It is that, incidentally, that explains why in the case of the former Yugoslavia the Secretary-General's report antedated the Statute. In the case of Rwanda his office, the Secretariat, did not draft the Statute, it was done by the Security Council, and the Secretary-General's report post-dates the Statute adopted and the establishment of the Tribunal. The Secretary-General in his reports for Rwanda and, as we will see, for the former Yugoslavia, did not rest content with this implicit approach. He was explicit with regard to whether it was internal or international armed conflict that was being considered. In paragraph 11 of the report of the Secretary-General, still dealing with document No. 31, page 3 paragraph 11, said: "Given the nature of the conflict as non-international in character, the Council has incorporated within the subject matter jurisdiction of the Tribunal violations of international humanitarian law which may either be committed in both the international and internal armed conflicts, such as the crime of genocide and crimes against humanity or may b committed only in internal armed conflict such as violations of Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions as more fully elaborated in Article 4 of Additional Protocol II." So it is against that background, in our submission, that one must come and consider the important resolutions dealing with the former Yugoslavia. Let me start in September 1991. The former Yugoslavia had clearly already begun to break up. That is notorious and appears from resolutions of the Security Council itself. The ten-day war in Slovenia was already over. Croatia and Slovenia had declared their independence from the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and fighting had begun in Croatia between the JNA and the Krajina Serbs. I mention those facts because it was in that context on 25th September 1991 that the Security Council acting under Chapter VII of the Charter imposed an arms embargo over the whole of Yugoslavia. That is in resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Prosecutor, do you mind I interrupt you and go back to what you were saying about the General Assembly resolutions before you start dealing with the question of the former Yugoslavia. If I understand you correctly, and judging from what you stated in your written response to the Defence, you start from the assumption that the Security Council makes a sort of watertight distinction in its resolutions between those cases where one is confronted with the international armed conflicts and those cases where there is simply an internal armed conflict. Actually you say on page 3 o your brief: "The Security Council refers to grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and to the general applicability of the Geneva Conventions only where it considers a conflict to be international. It refers to common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and additional Protocol II only where it considers a conflict to be internal." This is interesting, but I would like you to comment on the following facts. Actually if you look at the resolutions you have just quoted, in particular the resolutions of Rwanda, no mention is made of Article 3 in most of the resolutions. I would like to add that there are other Security Council resolutions which I cannot find here in this list of resolutions, namely quite a few on Somalia, Liberia and Jordan, three cases of internal armed conflict, where no mention at all is made of common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions. In those resolutions the Security Council simply pointed out that "Widespread violations of international humanitarian law were occurring in Somalia or Jordan", so I will not tax your patience with reading. I have here with me the text of these resolutions. Therefore, in a way what you pointed out on page 3 of your brief, I would like you to comment on that, is really not correct, because, as I say, whenever the Security Council resolution is confronted with some sort of internal disturbances, internal conflicts, it does not always or normally it refrains from referring to common Article 3 and simply draws the attention of the parties concerned to "widespread violations of international humanitarian law". This is one point The second point is if we could assume that the Security Council actually sticks to a very strict dichotomy, distinction between, say, international armed conflicts, and there it quotes the Geneva Conventions and grave breaches and so on, internal armed conflicts and in that respect it would only mention Article 3, would such a distinction be binding upon our Tribunal, namely, would our Tribunal be bound by any classification of the international or internal armed conflict given by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might answer the first question first. I must hasten to concede that the statement that appears on page 3 is too widely stated. It was intended to refer to the specific examples we gave dealing with the Israel/Jerusalem situation, the Iraq/Kuwait situation and contrasting Rwanda. We have not there dealt with the other examples which you have put to us. I would respectfully request you to read that statement in a far more narrow way than it is stated on page 3 of the brief. As far as the second and fundamental question is concerned, our main submission is that this Tribunal would be bound for the same reason really. It is connected very closely to the question of reviewability of the appointment of the Tribunal. If our submission is correct, and I am answering your question on that hypothesis because it is based on that hypothesis, the hypothesis is that the Security Council made this determination and the submission goes further, that it framed the Statute and passed the Statute on the basis o that determination. Again it is the question of the power of a sub-organ with regard to the body that established it. That would be our main submission. The alternative submission would be that if you were not bound by it, it is a matter to which full effect should be given in having a look and determining whether this decision was correct or not, whether it is a rational or irrational decision, an arbitrary or not an arbitrary decision. Our submission is that this gets very close to the question of reviewability by this Tribunal of decisions and acts of the Security Council. We would urge strongly, with respect, that the Security Council, subject to the determination of the opening date of the international armed conflict, was intending to confer on this Tribunal the wider jurisdiction conferred by the laws of international armed conflict and not limiting it for any relevant period to the narrower laws which would apply in the case of an internal armed conflict. It made that determination and, as we will endeavour to convince your Honours, it drafted the Statute on that fundamental and basic understanding and determination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you do not mind if I can follow up on this again. How would you interpret the statement made by the Security Council when our Statute was adopted? The statement by Ambassador Albright who said, "We understand that other members of the Council share our view regarding the following clarifications related to the Statute", and then she went on to say: "You [members of the Tribunal will have to apply also common Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions." If the Security Council, a prominent member of the Security Council, speaking to some extent on behalf of all the other members of the Security Council, also enjoins our Tribunal to apply Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions, one could argue that she implied that in case we were confronted with internal armed conflict we were at liberty to apply Article 3. That means she started from the assumption that we would also have to deal with internal armed conflict. In addition, how would you then interpret -- probably I am anticipating what you are going to say -- Article 5 of our Statute? Also how would we go about the agreement made by the conflicting parties on 22nd May 1992 based on common Article 3? That agreement could be interpreted only in one way, I think, but again I would be grateful if you could comment on that. Namely, all the parties concerned, including the essential authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, started from the assumption that they were involved in an internal armed conflict, that is why they were applying common Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am grateful for the question because it is something that we have obviously given attention. The submission we make really has its answer supplied by Article 5 itself, because Article 5 clearly contemplates that the Tribunal might be dealing with internal armed conflict. It says so expressly: "Armed conflict whether international or internal in character." The answer, we submit, lies firstly in the Security Council on the advice of the Secretary-General choosing a neutral date for the beginning of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, 1st January 1991. In our submission, the Security Council clearly recognised that already by 1st January 1991 there was conflict in the former Yugoslavia. What it left open for this Tribunal to determine, and that is in effect what the Secretary-General says in paragraph 62 of his report, the Security Council is leaving it open to this Tribunal to determine when the internal conflict was elevated to an international conflict. Whatever that date may be, whether it is June, July or May of 1991 or 1992, what Article 5 deals with, and what the parties may or may not have had in mind, one does not know what to impute to them, was that the jurisdiction of the Tribunal begins on 1st January. It does not begin only on the date that the conflict became international. So it must have been contemplated on our interpretation that there would be a period, or that there could be a period, between 1st January 1991 and the date that this Tribunal determines there was an international armed conflict this Tribunal would have to have jurisdiction to deal with internal armed conflicts. It may still happen at the end. It may be, and let us hope that sooner rather than later, that there is peace in the former Yugoslavia, but that serious violations of international humanitarian law are committed after the conflict has ceased to become international but during a period when the Security Council has seen fit to continue the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. It may choose a neutral date; it may wait. It may well be at the end of the international conflict that this Tribunal still has jurisdiction, and would need to exercise it according to the laws of international humanitarian law which apply to internal conflict. We submit this is the reason that Articles 2 and 3 clearly only deal with international armed conflicts, grave breaches and the war crimes referred to. In Article 4 genocide would apply to both, so nothing need be stated. In Article 5 it was necessary to be specific because the Security Council was narrowing crimes against humanity. In our submission, crimes against humanity, as they are now understood in international humanitarian law, would not necessarily be tied to war or to conflict. The Security Council was, in our submission, narrowing the jurisdiction of this Tribunal with regard to crimes against humanity by linking it to conflict, whether international or internal. It was in this respect presumably that it wanted this Tribunal to have jurisdiction to try people for crimes against humanity, not only during such periods after the conflict became or ceased to be international, but also during periods before it became international or it may be after it ceases to be international. So we submit that the factors which you point out, Mr. President, are not in any way inconsistent with the general submission we make with regard to the interpretation of the resolutions or the Statute of the Security Council. I was referring to the arms embargo over the whole of Yugoslavia. We would point out in this regard that to this day that embargo has not been lifted. This is the first indication perhaps of the approach of the Security Council of dealing with the former Yugoslavia globally or as a totality. By May 1992 the President of what had become the six republics met at The Hague under the auspices of the ICRC and agreed to respect the provisions of international humanitarian law. That was on 5th November 1991. The independence of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina had been widely recognised by the international community, and importantly Serbia and Montenegro had formed the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27th April 1992 as the successor state to the former SFRY. I mention that again to put in context resolution 752 which is at page 12 of the bundle. In 752 the Council expressly states that it considered the announcement in Belgrade, in what is now self-declared the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that the JNA had been withdrawn. That is in the middle of the right-hand column on the front page of 752. It is more significant that it continues to deal with the situation in the former Yugoslavia as a totality or globally. We submit it has continued to do that to this day. One sees that from page 2, paragraphs 3 and 4. I do not want to spend time reading them, but it is dealing there with the presence of the JNA. Notwithstanding statements to the contrary from Belgrade, it is demanding that interference from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, including units of the JNA as well as elements of the Croatian army, cease immediately and demanded that they be withdrawn. It continues to deal with UNPROFOR and the other matters in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, although not yet, interestingly enough, calling it the "former Yugoslavia", until in resolution 757 of 30th May 1992. Before I come to that resolution, again to put it in context, on 18th May, some twelve days earlier, the Security Council approved the membership of the United Nations of Croatia and Slovenia. Two days later it did the same in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It gave the approval so that the General Assembly could act formally and admit them to membership. The General Assembly did that on 22nd May. It admitted all three Republics as full members of the United Nations. On the same day, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia recognised Slovenia. It was in that context that one should consider the terms of what we submit is a very important resolution, 757, of 30th May 1992. If your Honours would look at it, it is, as I mentioned, No. 13 in the bundle. The Security Council started by “noting that in the very complex context of events in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, all parties bear some responsibility for the situation”. So now it is faced as a fait accompli with the breakup of the former SFRY, and it notes and deals with it as a totality. It talks about this complex context of events. It is causing deep concern to the international community and to the Security Council, and that all parties in the former Yugoslavia bear some responsibility for the situation. If I can skip the next paragraph and go to the following one, it says: "Deploring the fact that the demands in resolution 752 have not been complied with, including its demands that all parties and others concerned in Bosnia and Herzegovina stop the fighting immediately, that all forms of interference from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina cease immediately", recognising here second party interference in a state which it is already admitted to full membership of the United Nations, "that Bosnia and Herzegovina's neighbours take swift action to end all interference and respect the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina". If one turns over the page, one sees now the Security Council dealt with Bosnia and Herzegovina; it now deals with Croatia. In the middle of the page: "... deeply concerned also at developments in Croatia, including persistent cease fire violations and the continued expulsion of non-Serb civilians and of the obstruction of and lack of co-operation with UNPROFOR in other parts of Croatia." If I can go across to the second column, just below the centre of the page and point out that they then said that they "determine that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in other parts of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia constitutes a threat to international peace and security". So, again a global approach to the whole of the former Yugoslavia, that as a totality and consequent upon the breakup of the former Socialist Federal Republic, that global situation posed threat, constituted a threat, to international peace and security. If one continues the saga, on 20th June Bosnia and Herzegovina declared a state of war to exist in its territory. On following day, the Bosnian Croats declared their autonomy. Fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina had been escalating for some weeks. On 13th July 1992, in that context, resolution 764 at page 14, document 14 in the bundle, at the top of page 2, the Council said that "... deeply disturbed by the situation which now prevails in Sarajevo and by many reports and indications of deteriorating conditions throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina." So, here it was specifically dealing with the escalation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the next page, in paragraph 10, it reaffirms that "all parties are bound to comply with the obligations under International Humanitarian Law and, in particular, the Geneva Convention of 12th August 1949, and that persons who commit or order the commission of grave breaches of the Conventions are individually responsible in respect of such breaches." We submit here again, as we saw in the case of Israel, as we saw in the case of Kuwait, an implicit, not an explicit, determination of an international conflict existing in the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Those references one finds after this date with some repetition. In resolution 771 of 13th August 1992, at page 15, the Council again refers in paragraph 1 to the commission of grave breaches in the same terms, paragraph 1. In paragraph 2, it says: "... strongly condemns an violations of international humanitarian law, including those involved in the practice of ethnic cleansing." So, here it is dealing in consecutive paragraphs with grave breaches, ethnic cleansing. Then in 3 it demands that "all parties and others concerned in the former Yugoslavia and all military forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately cease and desist from all breaches of International Humanitarian Law, including from actions such as those described above." "Those described above" are those referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2. I stress, with respect, the fact that it is dealing still as a totality as it did without a single exception with the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Then, your Honours, on 6th October 1992 came the resolution to which I have already referred you, establishing the Commission of Experts, that is the resolution at document 16. I will not repeat the paragraphs which I drew to your attention in distinction to those dealing with Rwanda. I emphasise in this context that it established the Commission to investigate grave breaches in the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. On 16th November 1992, the Security Council authorised States, under its Chapter VII authority, to inspect maritime vessels from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to ensure compliance with the embargoes which the Security Council had imposed under Chapter VII on FRY. It is significant that in that context, in the context of embargoes, the enforcement of embargoes against one of the former republics of the SFRY, the Security Council in resolution of 16th November, resolution 787, document No. 18, there in paragraph 8 on the third page, it says: "... welcomes the establishment of the Commission of Experts provided for in paragraph 2 of resolution 780 and requests the Commission to pursue actively its investigations with regard to grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and other violations of International Humanitarian Law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in particular, the practice of ethnic cleansing." This is, as I say, in a resolution that was dealing with an economic embargo which had been imposed some time before on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On 26th January 1993, the Commission of Experts put in and submitted to the Security Council an interim report. In paragraph 45 of that report, the Commission discussed in paragraphs 41 to 45 the rules of International Humanitarian Law which would apply to the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia. I do not know if your Honours would like separate copies of that report? I do not think it appears in the documents. If I might ask leave to hand them in? (Handed) I see there is not an extra copy. We will make amends as soon as possible -- in fact, right now. I would like to refer only to one paragraph at page 14, paragraph 45. The Commission there stated that "it is of the opinion" -- however, it has now discussed the complex legal situation -- "that the character an complexity of the armed conflicts concerned combined with the web of agreements on humanitarian issues the parties have concluded amongst themselves, justify an approach whereby it applies the law applicable in international armed conflicts to the entirety of the armed conflicts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." Your Honours, I refer to that paragraph and to that report because on 22nd February, after it had received this report, the Security Council adopted resolution 808, document 19, in which it refers to that report. So, it is now cognisant of the attitude of the Commission of Experts in this regard which is completely in accord with its own implicit determination. But if I might refer you to resolution 808, because that is obviously a cardinal resolution in which the Council decided to establish this very Tribunal. It says there in the second paragraph on the left hand page at the beginning: "Recalling paragraph 10 of resolution 764, in which it reaffirmed that all parties are bound to comply with the obligations under international humanitarian law, in particular, the Geneva Conventions, and that persons who commit or order the commission of grave breaches of the Conventions are individually responsible in respect of such breaches." So it is recalling (a) its global treatment of the former Yugoslavia and it is repeating its implicit determination that it was dealing here with an international armed conflict. Going to the top of the second column: "Having considered the interim report of the Commission of Expert established by resolution 780, in which the Commission observed that a decision to establish an ad hoc international tribunal in relation to events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia would be consistent with the direction of its work, Expressing once again its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring within the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including reports of mass killings and the continuance of the practice of ‘ethnic cleansing’, [and] Determining that the situation constitutes a threat to international peace and security, Determined to put an end to such crimes and to take effective measures to bring to justice the persons who are responsible for them." So the crimes it is talking about in relation to establishing this Tribunal are crimes recognised by the international humanitarian laws relating to international conflicts. It says: " ... convinced that in the particular circumstances of the former Yugoslavia, the establishment of an international tribunal would enable the same to be achieved and would contribute to the restoration and maintenance of peace". Then in substantive paragraph 1 on the next page, it states that "an international tribunal shall be established for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991". Then, your Honours, the Secretary-General reported t the Security Council, as this resolution 808 instructed him to do. In his introduction to his report, the Secretary-General recalled a number of the previous resolutions and, in particular, he referred to those that refer to the commission of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. I refer here to paragraphs 5, 6 and 7 of the report of the Secretary-General. I do not need to read them out. He refers to resolutions to which I have already drawn attention. In paragraph 9, he refers to the finding by the Commission of Experts that grave breaches and other contraventions of international humanitarian law had been committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Then in paragraph 25, the Secretary-General states, inter alia, at the bottom of paragraph 25: "The Council has repeatedly reaffirmed that all parties in the former Yugoslavia are bound to comply with the obligations under international humanitarian law, in particular, the Geneva Conventions of 12th August 1949, and that persons who commit or order the commission of grave breaches of the conventions are individually responsible in respect of such breaches." So, he is repeating and is obviously drawing the attention of the Security Council to the very acts and implicit determinations which it had already made over the preceding period of many months. The Secretary-General then went on to discuss subject matter jurisdiction explicitly. At paragraphs 34 and 35, he deals with the principle of nullum crimen sine lege; requires that "the international tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law, so that the problem of adherence of some but not all states to specific Conventions does not arise". In 35, he says that "the part of conventional international humanitarian law which has beyond doubt become part of international customary law is the law applicable in armed conflicts as embodied in Geneva Conventions, The Hague Convention and the regulations annexed thereto, the Convention on Genocide and the Charter of the International Military Tribunal". Then he goes on to deal specifically with grave breaches and in paragraph 39 he says: "The Security Council has reaffirmed on several occasions that persons who commit or order the commission of grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions in the territory of the former Yugoslavia are individually responsible for such breaches as serious violations of international humanitarian law." So, he too is dealing with a totality. It, with respect, makes logical and rational sense because what was the Security Council dealing with but the effects, the unfortunate effects, of the breakup of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? In that context, we submit, must be read paragraph 62 where the Secretary-General was dealing with the temporal jurisdiction. He says: "With regard to temporal jurisdiction, the Security Council resolution 808 extends the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal to violations committed since 1991". It was not explicit about the date. "The Secretary-General understands this to mean any time on or after 1st January 1991. This is a neutral date which is not tied to any specific event an is clearly intended to convey the notion that no judgement as to the international or internal character of the conflict is being exercised." We submit that what that means (and it can only have one meaning in context) is that on a date subsequent to 1st January, the conflict became international in the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It follows, in our submission, that it must be for this Tribunal to decide that question, which is a mixed question of law and fact, as to the date on which the conflict in the former Yugoslavia became international. We submit, your Honours, that there are two possible approaches to that determination by this Tribunal as to when it became international. The one is to rely on notorious facts of which this Tribunal can in terms of its own rules of procedure and evidence take judicial notice and determine it was on a particular date, or we would submit the alternative open to the Tribunal would be to say that in this case we need go no further than to say that by the time the events alleged in the indictment against Mr. Tadic are concerned, by that date at least, the conflict had become international, without having to determine a precise date when it so became international. In our brief, we have set out facts which, in our submission, are notorious and which would enable this Appeals Chamber to come to the conclusion either to fix a date, or to decide in any event that by 24th May 1992 the conflict had become international, and that would mean that it was international before any of the events alleged against Mr. Tadic are alleged to have occurred Mr. President, your Honours, it remains only to deal very briefly with Article 5. It has really been covered in the opening submissions I made on judicial notice. In our submission, it is not open in a preliminary motion for the Defence to ask this Tribunal to take judicial notice of events which are, clearly, in dispute. It may well be that judicial notice may be properly taken, for example, of the paragraph that you, Mr. President, read to Mr. Orie. We would submit that if those facts are disputed by the Defence, then it is not a matter for judicial notice in all probability, but a matter to be proved appropriately before the Trial Chamber. That is a matter really where we are in the hands of the Defence. But we would submit it would be in the interests of justice for this Tribunal to come to a conclusion on the preliminary motions that we are dealing with, on facts which you can clearly take judicial notice of without having to rely on the consent of the parties. Such a judgement would have binding effect in respect of other indictments that may be issued. If one only has regard to facts which, because of happenstance, may not be contested by this or any other defendant, one is then really dealing ad hoc and the judgement would to that extent not be applicable to different times and to different defendants, to different accused. So, in short, Mr. President, your Honours, we would submit that the order which was made by the Trial Chamber should be affirmed on the basis that the determination b the Security Council that the conflict in the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia had become an international armed conflict prior to the dates relevant to the indictment of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. May I ask you a question relating to a point you have just made? Am I correct in saying that a few minutes ago you said that by 24th May 1992 the armed conflict had become in any case international?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If this is what you said, then how do you explain the fact that on 22nd May 1992 the parties concerned made an agreement in Geneva under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross based on Article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions, and they undertook to respect and apply -- I read Article 1: "The parties commit themselves to ensure respect for the Article 3 of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 which states", and then also further on they say they agree to bring into force other provisions of the Geneva Conventions. If they made this agreement on the basis of Article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions, the obvious implications would seem to be that they started from the assumption that they were involved in an internal armed conflict on 22nd May. So this agreement, of course, would be an agreement governing their future action.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, with submission for good reason, because a determination by the Security Council is one thing; the acceptance by all the parties of that determination is another. Certainly not many but a number of the parties did not recognise the independence even though it had been confirmed by the General Assembly of the United Nations. The Bosnian Serbs did not recognise the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It made good sense, certainly at least out of caution, to get an agreement under common Article 3 to have a concluded agreement binding the parties, whether or not they respected the decisions of the United Nations Security Council, to accept the relevant provisions of International Humanitarian Law. It was not left -- otherwise it would have been a very difficult situation where some parties recognised the applicability of the laws of international conflict and others did not. So it is in no way inconsistent with a determination by the Security Council in the manner we submit, on the one hand, and the parties, some of them ex abundante cautela, out of an abundance of caution, to enter into this agreement which would then be binding on all the parties, whether or not they recognised the independence inter se of each other.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With all due respect, I would seek consistency between what you stated in your written brief and the Security Council itself has already classified the conflict in the former Yugoslavia as an international one, this is what states ---

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- this is on page 3 at the top of your brief and this is what you stated also in your oral argument -- and then the attitude taken by the parties concerned, namely, the representative of Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic and the President of the Croatian Democratic Community. Their attitude was that actually this armed conflict was, indeed, not international, it was internal. Did you say that this is because they intended in this way, in a way recognised, that Bosnia and Herzegovina as such was a State? First of all, then I would comment that common Article 3, the last paragraph, provides that "the application of the preceding provisions shall not affect the legal status of the parties to the conflict".

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: This is the point, that they did not have to commit themselves publicly in a manner inconsistent with the views they had adopted with regard to recognition or non-recognition of other states. This really cut through political disputes about recognition.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One might argue that actually the fact that, say, a rebel faction or, say, a de facto government, as we say in international law, an authority fighting against the central authorities, by agreeing to apply common Article 3 implicitly challenges the authority of the central authority, the authority of the authorities in Sarajevo say, "We do not recognise the authority because we are rebels; we are fighting against you. We are fighting not against the State, we are fighting against an authority." Otherwise it would be an international armed conflict. If they say, "We are within the framework of an internal armed conflict", that means they do not recognise the authorities in Sarajevo as a representative of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would that not be consistent with the endeavour, that they went along with the endeavour of binding themselves willy-nilly; whether or not there was an international conflict or an internal conflict, they bound themselves to accept responsibility for the enforcement of the provisions of International Humanitarian Law to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think in your submission - I may be wrong; correct me -- you also referred to the fact that the Appellant has no appeal against the decision of the Trial Chamber vis-à-vis the question of the establishment of the -----

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Do you consider that as non-existent because the learned counsel for the Appellant has not touched on the matter? I think it is his duty and responsibility to tell us that his appeal to that matter is competent or you should expand this argument so that learned counsel for the Appellant can reply on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the only basis on which we submit it is not appealable is on, we submit, a proper interpretation and understanding of Rule 72B which only allows an interlocutory appeal on matters of lack of jurisdiction. It is a question of whether an attack on the legality of the creation of this Tribunal is properly referred to for the purpose of Rule 72B as the lack of jurisdiction. If it is, then it is appealable; if it is not, then they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: I would like to put both counsel on guard for tomorrow whether Article 24 or 25 of our own Statute doe give the Appellant a right of appeal regarding an order passed on the preliminary motion. Can you please look at it? We shall discuss it tomorrow. Perhaps you are not well prepared today, both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will conclude now for today and we will continue tomorrow afternoon at 2.00 p.m. sharp because we need some time tomorrow, so probably we will go on until 6.00 or 7.00. The Tribunal is in recess until 2 o'clock tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The proceedings adjourned until the following day at 2.00 p.m.)
